stem_md:
Let  $P(z)$  be a polynomial with real coefficients whose roots are covered by a disk of radius R. Prove that for any real number  $k$ , the roots of the polynomial  $nP(z)-kP'(z)$  can be covered by a disk of radius  $R+|k|$ , where  $n$  is the degree of  $P(z)$ , and  $P'(z)$  is the derivative of  $P(z)$ .


can anyone help me? It would also be extremely helpful if anyone could tell me where they've seen this type of problems.............Has it appeared in any mathematics competitions? Or are there any similar questions for me to attempt? Thanks in advance!
solution_md:
No need to assume that  $P$  is real.
We can do  $P\rightarrow cP$  where  $c\not=0$  hence we may assume that  $P$  is monic. Then  $P=(x-a_1)\cdots(x-a_n)$  with  $|a_i-p|\le R$  for some  $p$ . For  $k=0$  the statement is obvious hence we take  $k\in {\bf C}^*$  (it doesn't have to be real). Then  $nP(z)=kP'(z)\iff P(z)=P'(z)=0\vee \sum_1^n {1\over {z-a_i}}={n\over k}$ .
Suppose  $z$  is a solution to the given equation with  $|z-p|>R+k$ . Then   $|z-a_i|\ge |z-p|-|p-a_i|> k$  for all  $i$ . The first option for solutions is impossible, hence we have  $\sum_1^n {1\over {z-a_i}}={n\over k}$ . But each term has modulus  $<{1\over k}$ , contradiction by the triangle inequality.

stem_md: Let  $a>1.$  A uniform wire is bent into a form coinciding with the portion of the curve  $y=e^x$  for  $x\in [0,a]$ , and the line segment  $y=e^a$  for  $x\in [a-1,a].$  The wire is then suspended from the point  $(a-1, e^a)$  and a horizontal force  $F$  is applied to the point  $(0,1)$  to hold the wire in coincidence with the curve and segment. Show that the force  $F$  is directed to the right.
solution_md:
If  $d$  is the density per unit length, then the total mass of wire is  $d\left[1 + \int_{0}^{a} \sqrt{1 + e^{2x}} dx\right]$ . The moment about the  $y-$ axis is  $d\left(a - \frac{1}{2}\right) + d \int_{0}^{a} x \sqrt{1 + e^{2x}} dx$ . We require that the  $x-$ coordinate of the center of mass exceeds  $a - 1$ . In other words: $a - \frac{1}{2} + \int_{0}^{a} x \sqrt{1 + e^{2x}} dx > (a - 1)\left[ 1 + \int_{0}^{a} \sqrt{1 + e^{2x}} dx \right]$ .

Set  $f(a) = \int_{0}^{a} x \sqrt{1 + e^{2x}} dx - (a - 1) \int_{0}^{a} \sqrt{1 + e^{2x}} dx$ . Then we require  $f(a) > -\frac{1}{2}$  for all  $a > 1$ . Clearly,  $f(0) = 0$ . We try differentiating and we get  $f '(a) = \sqrt{1 + e^{2a}} - \int_{0}^{a} \sqrt{1 + e^{2x}}dx$ .

One possibility is to evaluate the integral explicitly (substitute  $y = e^{2x}$ , then  $z^2 = 1 + y$ , but we end up with a messy but doable integral). But it is maybe easier to approximate. We have  $1 + e^{2x} < 1 + e^{2x} + \frac{e^{-2x}}{4} = (e^{x} + e^{-x}/2)^2$ . So: $\int_{0}^{a} \sqrt{1 + e^{2x}}dx < \int_{0}^{a} e^{x} + e^{-x}/2 dx = e^{x} - e^{-x}/2|_{0}^{k} = e^{a} - e^{-a}/2 - 1/2 < e^{a} < \sqrt{1 + e^{2a}}$ ;

so  $f '(a) > 0$ . Hence  $\textcolor{red}{f(a) > f(0) > 0 > -\frac{1}{2}}$ .

stem_md: Given  $n$  points in the plane, show that the largest distance determined by these points cannot occur more than  $n$  times.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/MAA AMC/Putnam/1957 Putnam/2875782.json

candidates:
Induct on \(n\). If \(n=1\) then there are no distances at all. Now suppose that for some \(n>1\) there exist \(n\) points with at least \(n+1\) occurences of the largest distance \(d_{\max}\).
Let \(V\) denote the given point set. Note that there is a point in \(V\) which is at distance \(d_{\max}\) from at most one point of \(V\). Indeed, suppose the contrary. Then any vertex of the graph \(G=(V, E)\), where
\[E=\{ (u, v) \in V\times V: |u-v|=d_{\max}\}\]
has degree at least \(2\).
Note that at least one vertex \(t\) of \(G\) has degree at least \(3\) otherwise the number of edges will be \(2n/2<n+1\). Let \(u, v, w\in V\) be adjacent to \(t\). WLOG \(u,v,w\) occur in this order when rotating around \(t\). Since \(\deg v\ge 2\) there is a vertex \(s\in V\setminus\{t\}\) adjacent to \(v\). WLOG \(s\) and \(u\) lie in different sides of the line through \(v\) and \(t\). Then it is easy to see that \(|u-s|>d_{\max}\). This contradiction proves the existence of a vertex \(r\in V\) of degree at most \(1\).
Now consider the graph \(G\setminus\{r\}\). It has \(n-1\) vertices and \(d_{\max}\) occurs at least \(n\) times in its distances. However this is impossible according to the induction hypothesis. So our initial assumption is false and the problem is solved.
See also [here](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h1900222p12987439).

stem_md: Let  $a>0$ ,   $S_1 =\ln a$  and  $S_n = \sum_{i=1 }^{n-1} \ln( a- S_i )$  for  $n >1.$  Show that  $$  \lim_{n \to \infty} S_n = a-1. $$
solution_md:
If we hvae  $a=1$  then  $S_n=0\quad\forall n\in\mathbb{Z^+}$  so  $\lim_{n\to\infty} S_n=0=a-1$ .
If  $a\neq 1$  then we'll prove  $S_n<a-1\quad\forall n\in\mathbb{Z^+}$ .The case  $n=1$  is obviously true ( $\ln(a)<a-1$  with  $a\ne 1$ ).We have 2 cases: $\textbf{Case 1:}\  S_2<a-1$  
For positive integer  $k> 1$  if we have  $S_k<a-1$ , then  $$ S_{k+1}-S_k=\sum^{k}_{i=1}\ln(a-S_i)-\sum^{k-1}_{i=1}\ln(a-S_i)=\ln(a-S_k)\implies S_{k+1}=S_k+\ln(a-S_k)<S_k+a-S_k-1=a-1 $$  By induction, we have  $S_n<a-1$  for all positive integer  $n$   $(1)$ .
We also have  $S_n$  strictly increasing since   $$ S_{n+1}-S_n=\ln(a-S_n)>\ln(a-(a-1))=0\ (2) $$  By  $(1),(2)$  inffer that  $S_n$  must has limit, the equation if the limit is  $L=L+\ln(a-L)$  so that  $L=a-1$ , finish. $\textbf{Case 2:}\ S_2\geq a-1$  , If there isn't a positive integer  $n_0$  such that  $S_{n_0}<a-1$  then  $S_n\ge a-1$  for all positive  $n>1$  then  $S_{n+1}\leq S_n$  for  $n>1$  then  $S_n$  decreasing and  $S_n\geq a-1$  so it has limit  $L=a-1$ .
If there exists  $n_0$  such that  $S_{n_0}<a-1$  so  $S_k<a-1$  for  $k\in\mathbb{Z^+},k\geq n_0$ , similar to  $\textbf{case 1}$  we get  $\lim_{n\to\infty} S_n=a-1$ , the end the proof.

solution_md: Let  $\sigma\in\mathfrak S_{100}$ . Then  $\prod_{i=1}^{100}a_{\sigma(i)i}=\prod_{i=1}^{100}i\sigma(i)=100!100!$ . Since  $101$  is prime, then each element in  $1,...,100$  has a unique inverse  $\pmod{101}$  and so by grouping them together appropriately in the expression  $100!100!$  we get  $\prod_{i=1}^{100}a_{\sigma(i)i}\equiv1\pmod{101}$  as wanted

stem_md: For  $f(x)$  a positive , monotone decreasing function defined in  $[0,1],$  prove that  $$  \int_{0}^{1} f(x) dx \cdot \int_{0}^{1} xf(x)^{2} dx \leq \int_{0}^{1} f(x)^{2} dx \cdot \int_{0}^{1} xf(x) dx. $$
solution_md:

stem_md: The curve  $y=y(x)$  satisfies  $y'(0)=1.$  It satisfies the differential equation  $(x^2 +9)y'' +(x^2 +4)y=0.$  Show that it crosses the  $x$ -axis between  $$ x= \frac{3}{2} \pi \;\;\; \text{and} \;\;\; x= \sqrt{\frac{63}{53}} \pi. $$
solution_md:
We compare the equation given with (1)  $z'' = -4z/9, z(0) = 0, z'(0) = 1$ , and (2)  $w'' = -53w/63, w(0) = 0, w'(0) = 1$ .

For all  $x > 0$  we have  $(x^2 + 4)/(x^2 + 9) > 4/9$ , so  $y''z - yz'' = (4/9 - (x^2 + 4)/(x^2 + 9) ) yz$ . Integrating gives  $y'z - yz'$ |03π/2 = ∫  $(4/9 - (x^2 + 4)/(x^2 + 9) ) yz dx$  (*). Now  $y(0) = z(0) = 0, z = sin 2x/3$ , so  $z(3\pi/2) = 0, z'(3\pi/2) = -2/3$ , hence  $y'z - yz'$ |03π/2  $= 2/3 y(3\pi/2)$ . Now if y has no zeros on the open interval  $(0, 3\pi/2)$ , then  $y(3\pi/2)$  ≥  $0$  and the integrand  $(4/9 - (x^2 + 4)/(x^2 + 9) ) yz$  is negative for the entire interval. Hence lhs (*) ≥  $0$  and rhs (*) <  $0$ . Contradiction. So  $y$  has at least on zero on  $(0, 3\pi/2)$ .

Turning to (2), we note that  $2\pi < 10$ , so  $(3\pi/2)2 < 22.5$ . Hence on the interval  $[0, 3\pi/2]$  we have  $(x^2 + 4)/(x^2 + 9) < 26.5/31.5 = 53/63$ . Now  $w = sin (\sqrt{53/63}x)$ , so  $w(x) > 0$  on the interval  $(0, k)$ , where  $k = \sqrt{63/53}\pi$ .

Now suppose that y has a root in  $(0, k]$ . Let  $h$  be the smallest such root, so that  $y(x)$  is positive on  $(0, h)$  and  $y(h) = 0, y'(h)$  ≤  $0$ . Integrate  $w''y - w y'' = ( (x^2 + 4)/(x^2 + 9) - 53/63)$ . The lhs is  $w'y - w y'$  |0h  $= w(h) y'(h)$  ≥  $0$ . The rhs is ∫ $0h ( (x^2 + 4)/(x^2 + 9) - 53/63) y w dx$ . But the integrand is negative on  $(0, h)$ , so the rhs <  $0$ . Contradiction. Hence  $y$  has no roots on  $(0, k]$ . So, it must have a root on  $(k, 3\pi/2)$ .

stem_md: Title is self explanatory. Pick two points on the unit sphere. What is the expected distance between them?
solution_md:
My solution is essentially the same as Neighbor's approach, but I didn't use a surface integral.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>**Claim:** If we randomly choose a point uniformly on a sphere  $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$  and getting its  $x$ -coordinate, this is just equivalent to randomly choosing a number uniformly from  $[-1,1]$ .**Proof:** I have a proof for this, but it's quite long. But I think this was also proven on a 3Blue1Brown video about the formula of a sphere's surface area, and that one's much nicer.
[rule]
Without loss of generality, suppose that one of the points lies at  $(-1,0,0)$ , and the other point be  $(x,y,z)$ , where  $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ . The distance between the two points is  $$ \sqrt{(x+1)^2+y^2+z^2}=\sqrt{x^2+2x+1+y^2+z^2}=\sqrt{2+2x} $$  This shows that the distance between the two points really only depends on what the value of  $x$  is. Furthermore, according to the Claim above, we know that  $x$  is a random variable uniformly chosen from  $[-1,1]$ . Therefore, the expected distance is given by the integral:  $$ \frac12\int_{-1}^1\sqrt{2+2x}\,\mathrm dx=\boxed{\frac43} $$</details>

stem_md: Two uniform solid spheres of equal radii are so placed that one is directly above the other. The bottom sphere is fixed, and the top sphere, initially at rest, rolls off. At what point will contact between the two spheres be "lost"? Assume the coefficient of friction is such that no slipping occurs.
solution_md:
*Yes, this problem has already been solved and the solution is good, but I would like to offer a simpler solution, one might say, a solution from school*

The center of the upper sphere moves along a circle of radius  $2R$ . The angular velocity of rotation of the upper sphere around its center  $\omega$  is related to the angular velocity of the center of mass  $\Omega$  by the relation  $\omega = 2\Omega$  (from the condition of no slip). The potential energy of the upper sphere is transformed into kinetic energy of translational and rotational motion. Change in potential energy is  $2mgR(1 - \cos \theta)$ . Kinetic energy: translational  $\frac{1}{2} \cdot m(2R\Omega)^2$  and rotational  $\frac{1}{2} \cdot I(2\Omega)^2$ , where moment of inertia  $I = \frac{2}{5} \cdot mR^2$ . Now let's use the energy conservation equation  $$ 2mgR(1 - \cos \theta) = \frac{14}{5}mR^2\Omega^2 \Rightarrow \Omega^2 = \frac{10g(1 - \cos \theta)}{14R} $$  The centripetal acceleration  $a = 2R\Omega^2$ , and the equation of motion in the radial direction is  $N = mg \cos \theta - 2mR\Omega^2$ . Let's substitute  $\Omega^2$  from the law of conservation of energy  $$ N = mg \cos \theta - \frac{20mg(1 - \cos \theta)}{14} \Rightarrow N = \frac{mg}{7}(17 \cos \theta - 10) $$  Since  $N = 0$  (condition of contact loss), then  $$ 17 \cos \theta - 10 = 0 \Rightarrow \cos \theta = \frac{10}{17} \Rightarrow \theta = \arccos \frac{10}{17} $$

Taking moments about an axis through  $X$  yields  $MgR\sin(\theta) = I \frac{d^{2}\theta}{dt^2}$  (ii), where  $I$  is the moment of inertia of the sphere about  $X \Rightarrow$  the moment about a diameter  $+ MR^2 = \frac{7}{5}MR^2$ .

stem_md: Real numbers are chosen at random from the interval  $[0,1].$  If after choosing the  $n$ -th number the sum of the numbers so chosen first exceeds  $1$ , show that the expected value for  $n$  is  $e$ .
solution_md:
There is another approach, which admittedly is a bit more complicated than Tintarn's solution. Its advantage is that it works equally well for different distributions and variations of the problem. This approach is a classical exercise in using conditioning. 

First note that in the problem statement it should say: 'real numbers are chosen independently and uniformly in [0,1]'. 

For our approach let  $X_i$  denote the sequence of real numbers,  $N_a$  the number of reals need to exceed  $a$  for some  $a \in [0,1]$  and let  $f(a)$  denote the expectation of  $N_a$ . We compute  $f(a)$  by conditioning on  $X_1$ . We note that we are done if  $X_1 > a$ , and otherwise the subsequent numbers need to exceed  $a-X_1$ . Using the tower property of conditional expectation (and the distribution of the sequence  $X_i$ ) this gives   $$ f(a) = 1 + \int_0^a f(a-x) dx, \qquad \text{ i.e. } f(a) = 1 + \int_0^a f(t) dt.  $$   
This implies that  $f'(a) = f(a)$ , i.e.  $f(a) = c e^a$ , and since  $f(0) = 1$ , we get  $f(a) = e^a$  and in particular  $f(1) = e$ . 

Note that some details are left out in the above solution. We need to show that for all  $a$  we have  $f(a) < \infty$  (which follows by a crude estimate of the tail of  $N_a$ ) and  $f$  is differentiable (which follows from  $f(t) \le f(1) < \infty$  for  $t \in [0,1]$  and the above integral equation).

stem_md: Show that the integral equation  $$ f(x,y) = 1 + \int_{0}^{x} \int_{0}^{y} f(u,v) \, du \, dv $$  has at most one solution continuous for  $0\leq x \leq 1, 0\leq y \leq 1.$
solution_md:
Write  $(u,v)<(x,y)$  if  $u<x$  and  $v<y$ . Denote  $v_n=(x_n,y_n)$ , and  $dv_n=dx_ndy_n$ . Assume all vectors satisfies  $(0,0)\le v\le (1,1).$  It suffices to show that the equation  $Tu=u$  has unique solution  $u=0$ , where  $$ Tu(v):=\int_{\{w<v\}}f(w)dw. $$  Indeed, if  $Tu=u$ , then  $T^nu=u$ . For  $u\ne0$ , assume  $\|u\|_\infty=1$ , hence  $$ \begin{aligned}
\|T^nu\|_\infty&=\sup_{v}\int_{v_1<v}dv_1\int_{v_2<v_1}dv_2\cdots\int_{v_n<v_{n-1}}u(v_n)dv_n
&\le\int_{v_1<1}dv_1\int_{v_2<v_1}dv_2\cdots\int_{v_n<v_{n-1}}dv_n
&=\int_{v_1<1}dx_1dy_1\int_{v_2<v_1}dx_2dy_2\cdots\int_{v_n<v_{n-1}}dx_ndy_n=\frac1{(n!)^2}<1=\|u\|_\infty,
\end{aligned} $$  contradiction.

Indeed it suffices to consider for  $n=2$ , i.e.,  $T(Tu)\ne u$ .

stem_md: What is the smallest amount that may be invested at interest rate  $i$ , compounded annually, in order that one may withdraw  $1$  dollar at the end of the first year,  $4$  dollars at the end of the second year,  $\ldots$  ,  $n^2$  dollars at the end of the  $n$ -th year, in perpetuity?
solution_md: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. The present value of one dollar to be paid after $n$ years is $(1 + i)^{-n}$ dollars. Hence the value in dollars of the given annuity is \[\sum^\infty_{n=1} n^2 (1 + i)^{-n}.\] Since \[\frac 1{1 -x} = \sum^\infty_{n=0} x^n,\] we have \[\frac x{(1 - x)^2} = x \,\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx} \left(\frac 1{1-x}\right)=\sum^\infty_{n=1}nx^n\] and \[\frac{x + x^2}{(1 - x)^3} = \frac x{(1 - x)^2} = x \,\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx} \left(\frac x{(1-x)^2}\right) = \sum^\infty_{n=1} n^2 x^n\] for $|x|<1.$ Putting $x = \dfrac 1{1 + i},$ we obtain \[\sum^\infty_{n=1} n^2 (1 + i)^{-n} = \frac{(1 + i)(2 + i)}{i^3}.\] (At $6$ percent interest, the cost of the annuity would be $\$ 10{,}109.26.$)

stem_md: Show that ten equal-sized squares cannot be placed on a plane in such a way that no two have an interior point in common and the first touches each of the others.
solution_md: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. Suppose that such a set of unit squares exists. Let $S,S_1,S_2$ be three of the non-overlapping squares with centers respectively at $C, C_1,C_2$ and suppose $S$ touches both $S_1$ and $S_2.$ Let $\theta = \measuredangle C_1 CC_2,$ $a = |C_1 C|,$ $b= |CC_2|,$ $c = |C_2C_1|.$ Then $1 \le a \le \sqrt2,$ $1 \le b \le \sqrt2,$ and $c \ge 1.$ By the law of cosines \[\cos \theta = \frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}\le\frac{a^2+b^2-1}{2ab}=f(a,b).\]\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial a}=\frac{a^2-b^2+1}{2a^2b} \text{ and } \frac{\partial f}{\partial b} = \frac{b^2-a^2+1}{2ab^2}.\] Both of these derivatives are non-negative throughout the allowable $(a, b)$ domain, so it follows that the maximum value of $f$ on that domain is $f(\sqrt2, \sqrt2) = 3/4.$ Thus $\cos \theta \le 3/4$ and $\theta \ge \arccos 3/4.$ Let $\alpha = \arccos 3/4.$ Then \[\cos 3\alpha = 4\cos^3\alpha-3\cos\alpha=-\frac9{16}<-\frac12=\cos\frac{2\pi}3.\]Hence $3\alpha>2\pi/3,$ and so $\measuredangle C_1 CC_2 = \theta \ge \alpha > 2\pi/9.$ Now suppose that $S,S_1,S_2,S_3,\ldots,S_9$ are the non-overlapping squares, with $S$ touching each of the others. Let $C,C_1,C_2,C_3,\ldots,C_9$ be the respective centers. Choose polar coordinates with center at $C,$ and number the squares so that the angular coordinates of $C_1,C_2,\ldots,C_9$ increase monotonically between $0$ and $2\pi.$ Then \[\measuredangle C_1 CC_2 + \measuredangle C_2 CC_3 + \cdots + \measuredangle C_9 CC_1 = 2\pi,\] so at least one of these nine angles is no greater than $2\pi/9,$ contrary to what we have proved above. Hence the configuration is impossible.

stem_md: Prove that the product of four consecutive positive integers cannot be a perfect square or cube.
solution_md:
It's apparently a theorem of Erdős that the product of consecutive integers can't be a perfect power. Of course, this particular case can also be nuked with Catalan's (which wasn't proven in 1958), since  $n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)=(n^2+3n+1)^2-1$ .

Indeed, if  $P=n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)$ , then  $P+1$  is always a square (see above), so  $P$  itself cannot be a square (the only consecutive squares are  $0,1$ ). The more complicated part is to show that  $P$  cannot be a cube.

For this, observe that if  $p$  divides more than one of  $n,n+1,n+2,n+3$ , then  $p=2,3$ . Hence, all the numbers  $n,n+1,n+2,n+3$  are perfect cubes if we disregard factors of  $2$  and  $3$ .
Now it's easy to see (mod  $6$ ) that every four consecutive integers contain an integer coprime to  $6$ . Hence, by above discussion, one of  $n,n+1,n+2,n+3$  must be a perfect cube.

If  $P$  and  $n+3$  are perfect cubes, then  $P/(n+3)=n(n+1)(n+2)$  must be a perfect cube as well. However, this number is between  $n^3$  and  $(n+1)^3$ . We handle the other cases analogously: $(n+1)^3<n(n+2)(n+3)<(n+2)^3$  and  $(n+1)^3\leq n(n+1)(n+3)<(n+2)^3$  with equality only for  $n=1$ , which can be checked to fail. Finally,  $(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)$  is the same as  $n(n+1)(n+2)$  shifted by  $1$ .

stem_md: Prove that if  $f(x)$  is continuous for  $a\leq x \leq b$  and  $$ \int_{a}^{b} x^n f(x) \, dx =0 $$  for  $n=0,1,2, \ldots,$  then  $f(x)$  is identically zero on  $a \leq x \leq b.$
solution_md:
This is quite classical:
So  $\int_a^b P(x)f(x) dx=0$  for all polynomials  $P$ .
For any  $\varepsilon>0$ , by Weierstraß Approximation we can find  $P$  such that  $\vert P(x)-f(x)\vert<\varepsilon$  for all  $x \in [a,b]$ . Hence
\[\int_a^b f(x)^2 dx<\varepsilon\]
for all  $\varepsilon>0$ , hence the LHS is  $0$  and hence  $f$  is identically  $0$  by non-negativity of the integrand.

stem_md: Let  $R_1 =1$  and  $R_{n+1}= 1+ n\slash R_n$  for  $n\geq 1.$  Show that for  $n\geq 1,$   $$  \sqrt{n} \leq R_n \leq \sqrt{n} +1. $$
solution_md:
Just induction:
True for  $n=1$ . If true for  $n$ , then
\[R_{n+1} \le 1+\frac{n}{\sqrt{n}}=1+\sqrt{n}<1+\sqrt{n+1}\]
and
\[R_{n+1} \ge 1+\frac{n}{\sqrt{n}+1} >1+\frac{n}{\sqrt{n+1}+1}=1+(\sqrt{n+1}-1)=\sqrt{n+1}.\]

stem_md: Let  $a$  and  $b$  be relatively prime positive integers,  $b$  even. For each positive integer  $q$ , let  $p=p(q)$  be chosen so that  $$  \left| \frac{p}{q} - \frac{a}{b}  \right| $$  is a minimum. Prove that  $$  \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{q=1 }^{n} \frac{ q\left| \frac{p}{q} - \frac{a}{b}  \right|}{n} = \frac{1}{4}. $$
solution_md: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. Rewrite $q |p/q - a/b|$ in the form \[\frac 1b |pb - qa|.\] For each $q$ we are to choose $p$ to minimize this; then $pb - qa$ will be the absolutely least residue of $qa \pmod b.$ Since $a$ is relatively prime to $b,$ as $q$ varies through a complete set of residues $\pmod b,$ so will $qa,$ and therefore $pb - qa$ will take the values \[-C+1, -C+2,\ldots, -1, 0, 1,\ldots, C-1,C\] where $b = 2C$ (recall that $b$ is even) and the contribution to the sum will be \[\frac 1b (0 + 1 + 2 + \cdots + C - 1 + C + C - 1 + \cdots + 1) = \frac {C^2}{2C} = \frac b4.\] Thus if $n = b \cdot r + s$ where $0 \le s < b,$ we have \[\sum^n_{q=1} q \left| \frac pq - \frac ab \right| = r \frac b4 + \sum^{br + s}_{q = br + 1} q \left| \frac pq - \frac ab \right|\] since $q$ runs through $r$ complete residue systems ${\pmod b}$ and then the integers $br + 1, br + 2, \ldots, br + s.$ Since $p(q)$ is the integer nearest to $qa/b,$ \[q \left| \frac pq - \frac ab \right| = \left| p - \frac{qa}b\right| \le \frac 12.\] We have therefore \begin{align*} \left| \frac 14 n - \sum^n_{q=1} q \left| \frac pq - \frac ab \right| \right| &= \left| \frac s4 - \sum^{br + s}_{q = br + 1} q \left|\frac pq - \frac ab \right|\right| & \le \frac s4 + s \sup_q q \left| \frac pq - \frac ab \right| &\le \frac 34 x < \frac 34 b.\end{align*} Dividing by $n,$ we get \[ \left|\frac 14 - \frac 1n \sum^n_{q=1} q \left| \frac pq - \frac ab \right|\right| < \frac {3b}{4n}.\] Letting $n \to \infty,$ we see that \[\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac 1n \sum^n_{q=1} q \left| \frac pq - \frac ab \right| = \frac 14.\]

stem_md: Show that if a unit square is partitioned into two sets, then the diameter (least upper bound of the distances between pairs of points) of one of the sets is not less than  $\sqrt{5} \slash 2.$  Show also that no larger number will do.
solution_md:
Suppose otherwise that there exist non-empty  $A, B \subseteq [0, 1]^2$  such that both  $\operatorname{diam}(A)$  and  $\operatorname{diam}(B)$  is less than  $\sqrt{5}/2$ .

Then  $(0, 0)$  and  $(1, 1)$  cannot lie in the same set, because the distance between them is  $\sqrt{2}>\sqrt{5}/2$ ). Likewise  $(0, 1)$  and  $(1, 0)$  are not contained in the same set. So by the symmetry, we may assume that  $(0, 0)$  and  $(0, 1)$  lie in  $A$  and  $(1, 0)$  and  $(1, 1)$  lie in  $B$ .

Now consider the point  $p = (\tfrac{1}{2}, 1)$ . Since  $\operatorname{dist}((0, 0), p) = \sqrt{5}/2 = \operatorname{dist}((1, 0), p)$ , we must have  $p \notin A$  and  $p \notin B$ , a contradiction.

To show that  $\sqrt{5}/2$  is optimal, consider  $A = [0, 1]\times[0,\tfrac{1}{2}]$  and  $B=[0, 1]\times(\tfrac{1}{2}, 1]$ .

stem_md: Let  $C$  be a real number, and let  $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$  be a three times differentiable function such that  $$  \lim_{x \to \infty} f(x)=C, \;\; \; \lim_{x \to \infty} f'''(x)=0. $$  Prove that  $$  \lim_{x \to \infty} f'(x) =0 \;\; \text{and} \;\; \lim_{x \to \infty} f''(x)=0. $$
solution_md:
By Taylor's theorem, for all  $x \in \mathbb{R}$ ,  $h > 0$  there exists  $\xi \in (x, x+h)$  such that  $$ f(x+h)-f(x) = h f'(x) + h^2 \frac{f''(x)}{2} + h^3 \frac{f''' ( \xi ) }{6}. $$  This yields for all  $x \in \mathbb{R}$ ,  $h>0$   $$ \left| h f'(x) +  h^2 \frac{f''(x)}{2}\right| \le | f(x+h)-f(x)| + \frac{h^3}{6} | f''' ( \xi ) | . $$  For fixed  $h>0$  the RHS tends to zero as  $x \to \infty$ , since  $\xi > x$  and  $f \to C$ ,  $f''' \to 0$ .
In particular, with  $h=1$  we get  $f'(x) +  \frac{f''(x)}{2} \to 0$  and with  $h=2$  we get  $2 ( f'(x) + f'' ( x ) ) \to 0$ . This implies the claim.

stem_md: Let a complete oriented graph on  $n$  points be given. Show that the vertices can be enumerated as  $v_1 , v_2 ,\ldots, v_n$  such that  $v_1 \rightarrow v_2 \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow v_n.$
solution_md: We proceed by induction.  $n = 2$  is trivially true, so we proceed by the inductive step. Note that  $v_1$ ,  $v_2, \cdots v_{n-1}$  form a satisfactory chain by the inductive hypothesis. If  $v_n \rightarrow v_1$ , we are done. Otherwise, we must have  $v_1 \rightarrow v_n$ . In that case, check if  $v_n \rightarrow v_2$ . If so, we are done. If not, continue down the chain. Eventually, we get to testing if  $v_n \rightarrow v_{n-1}$ . If this is true, then place  $v_n$  between  $v_{n-2}$  and  $v_{n-1}$ . If this is not true, then place  $v_n$  at the end of the chain, and so we are done.  $\blacksquare$

Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press.**First solution.** We shall prove this by induction of $n.$ It is obviously true for $n = 2$ (and vacuously true for $n = 1$ ). We assume the result for $n = 1, 2, \ldots, k$ and consider a complete oriented graph on $k + 1$ points. Pick any one of these points, say $b,$ and consider two subsets of the remaining $k$ points \[A = \{x: x \to b\}, \; C = \{x: b - x\}.\] Then $A$ and $C,$ with the given directions for their pairs, are complete oriented graphs having, say, $p$ and $q$ points, respectively; $p + q = k.$ By the induction hypothesis $A$ can be enumerated so that $a_1 \to a_2 \to \cdots \to a_p,$ and $C$ can be enumerated so that $c_1 \to c_2 \to \cdots \to c_q.$ Then the required chain is given by \[a_1 \to a_2 \to \cdots \to a_p -\to b \to c_1 \to c_2 \to \cdots \to c_q.\] [Note that either $A$ or $C$ might be empty, but this creates no difficulty.

Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press.**Second solution**. Again assume that the result is true for $n = k$ points, and let a complete oriented graph $G$ on $k + 1$ points be given. Pick any point $b$ of $G.$ By the inductive hypothesis, the remaining $k$ points can be labeled $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k$ so that \[a_1 \to a_2 \to \cdots \to a_k.\] Then $b$ can be fitted into this sequence either just before $a_i,$ where $i$ is the least index with $b \to a_i,$ or at the end of the sequence if no such index exists.

stem_md: Let  $a_1 ,a_2 ,\ldots, a_n$  be a permutation of the integers  $1,2,\ldots, n.$  Call  $a_i$  a *big* integer if  $a_i >a_j$  for all  $i<j.$  Find the mean number of big integers over all permutations on the first  $n$  postive integers.
solution_md: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press.**Second Solution.** The average number of big integers in a permutation of $n$ distinct integers is the same no matter what these integers are. Call this number $A_n.$ Given a permutation of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\},$ remove the element $1$ and close up to obtain a permutation of $\{2, 3, \ldots, n \}.$ This defines an $n$ -to- $1$ mapping $\xi$ of permutations of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ into permutations of $\{2, 3, \ldots, n\}.$ If the element $1$ appeared at the end of the original permutation $\sigma,$ then $\xi(\sigma)$ has one big integer fewer than $\sigma.$ In all other cases $\xi (\sigma)$ has the same number of big integers as $\sigma.$ If $N(\sigma)$ denotes the number of big integers in $\sigma,$ this means that \[N(\sigma) = N(\xi(\sigma)) + 1 \text{ for } (n - 1)! \text{ permutations }\sigma\] and \[N(\sigma) = N(\xi(\sigma)) \text{ for the remaining permutations.}\] Hence \[\sum_\sigma N(\sigma) = \sum_n N(\xi(\sigma)) + (n - 1)!.\] Dividing through by $n!$ we see that \[A_n = \frac 1{n!} \sum_\sigma N(\xi(\sigma)) + \frac 1n.\] Since the mapping $\xi$ is always exactly $n$ -to- $1,$ \[\frac 1{n!} \sum_\sigma N(\xi(\sigma)) = A_{n-1}.\] This gives the recurrence \[A_n = A_{n-1} + \frac 1n.\] Since $A_1 = 1,$ it follows that \[A_n = 1 + \frac 12 + \frac 13 + \cdots + \frac 1n.\]

candidates: Final Putnam problem  :)

The probability that the  $k$ th number is big is the probability that it is the maximum in the last  $n-k+1$  elements, which is  $\frac{1}{n-k+1}$ . By linearity of expectation, the answer is then  $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n}$ .

A recursive solution. Let  $E(n)$  be the expected number of "big" integer of a permutation of the first  $n$  naturals.  $E(1)=1$  trivially. We can condition on the position of the placement of the nth number. It is in the first spot with probability  $1/n$ , and in this case the expectation is  $1+E(n-1)$ , as it is greater than all numbers after it and it's placement doesn't affect the "big"-ness of the last  $(n-1)$  numbers.   The nth number is not in the first spot with probability  $(n-1)/n$ , whatever number is in the first spot, it will not be "big" since "n" is after it. Note however since we have a permutation the actual numbers don't matter, only their relative magnitude. So the expected number of big numbers in the last  $(n-1)$  spots is still  $E(n-1)$ . Therefore the recurrence(by the law of total expectation) is  $E(n)=(1/n)*(E(n-1)+1)+(n-1)/n * (E(n-1)) = E(n-1)+1/n$ . So  $E(n)$  is the nth harmonic number.

Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press.**First Solution.** If $\sigma$ is a permutation, let $N_i (\sigma)$ be the number of "big" integers occurring at position $i.$ Then $N_i (\sigma)=0$ or $1.$ The average value of $N_i(\sigma)$ over all the permutations is $\dfrac 1{n-i+1}$ because after $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{i-1}$ have been selected, the question of whether or not $a_i$ will be a big integer is whether or not $a_i$ is the greatest among the $(n - i + 1)$ integers left. Let the number of big integers in $\sigma$ be $N(\sigma).$ Then $N(\sigma) = N_1 (\sigma) + N_2 (\sigma) + \cdots + N_n (\sigma),$ and the average value of $N(\sigma)$ over all the $n!$ permutations will be the sum of the average values of the separate terms, $N_i (\sigma),$ for $i = 1,2,\ldots, n.$ Hence this average is \[\frac 1n + \frac 1{n-1} + \frac 1{n-2} + \cdots + 1.\]

stem_md:
Hi everybody!
I've an interesting problem!
Can you solve it?

Prove **Erdös-Ginzburg-Ziv Theorem**: *"Among any  $2n-1$  integers, there are some  $n$  whose sum is divisible by  $n$ ."*
solution_md:
Here is a relatively elementary proof:

We first prove for  $n$  being a prime. We assume otherwise. Let  $p_1,...,p_{2n-1}$  be the numbers. Then consider the sum  $\sum{(p_{i_1}+...+p_{i_n})^{n-1}}$  over all set of  $p_i$  with  $n$  elements. Then by Fermat's little theorem, the sum is  $\equiv \dbinom{2n-1}{n}\not \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$ . We now consider the coefficients of the sum when the whole thing is expanded. Note that for any set of  $0<k<n$  of the numbers, it is a subset of exactly  $\dbinom{2n-1-k}{n-k}$  different sets in the sum. But since  $n|\dbinom{2n-1-k}{n-k}$ , all the coefficients in that sum is divisible by  $n$ , a contradiction. Thus we are done for primes.

Now suppose it is true for  $n=a,b$ . Then we show that it is also true for  $n=ab$ . Consider  $2ab-1$  numbers. We pick  $2a-1$  of them, choose  $a$  of them whose sum is divisible by  $a$ , and throw back the other  $a-1$  into the original set. We can keep doing this  $2b-1$  number of times, and let  $s_1,...,s_{2b-1}$  be the sum of the groups of  $a$ . We consider the numbers  $\frac{s_i}{a}$ , and out of the  $2b-1$  of them, we can choose  $b$  of them such that  $b|\sum^b{\frac{s_i}{a}}$ , thus  $ab|\sum^b{s_i}$ . So now we have  $ab$  numbers whose sum is divisible by  $ab$ . Thus by induction, it is true for all  $n$ .

stem_md:
Let  $\alpha$  and  $\beta$  be irrational numbers with the property that   $$ \frac{1}{\alpha} +\frac{1}{\beta}=1 $$  Let $\{a_n\}$  and  $\{b_n\}$  be the sequences given by  $a_n= \lfloor n\alpha \rfloor$  and  $b_n= \lfloor n\beta \rfloor$  respectively. Prove that the sequences  $\{ a_n\}$  and  $\{ b_n \} $  has no term in common and cover all the natural numbers.


I know this theorem from long ago, but forgot the proof of it. Can anybody help me with this?
solution_md:
Here's a somewhat large but naturally deducible proof of Beatty's theorem I had typed up a few years back.
<details><summary>Hidden for length</summary>We first do away with a quick substitution. Let  $\frac{1}{\alpha}=x$  and  $\frac{1}{\beta}=y$ . Then the two sequences become  $(x_n)=\lfloor n/x\rfloor$  and  $(y_n)=\lfloor n/y \rfloor$ . Now  $x+y=1$ . Without loss of generality, let  $x>\frac{1}{2}$  and  $y<\frac{1}{2}$ .
First we prove that the sequences are disjoint. Suppose that for some  $m,k\in\mathbb{N}$  such that  $m\ne k$  we have  $\left\lfloor \frac{m}{x}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor \frac{k}{y}\right\rfloor$ . From  $x>1/2$  and  $y<1/2$ , we have  $\frac{m}{x}<2m$  and  $\frac{k}{y}>2k$ . Now  $$ \left\lfloor \frac{m}{x}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor \frac{k}{y}\right\rfloor $$  gives us  $$ \frac{k}{y}-\frac{m}{x}=\left\{\frac{k}{y} \right\}-\left\{\frac{m}{x} \right\}. $$  Note that  $\left|\frac{k}{y}-\frac{m}{x}\right|\ge |2k-2m|=2|k-m|\ge 2$ . However we also have  $-1\le \left\{\frac{k}{y} \right\}-\left\{\frac{m}{x} \right\}<1$ .
So the only possibility is  $m=k$  which gives  $\left\lfloor \frac{k}{y}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor \frac{k}{x}\right\rfloor$ . But this is not possible since  $\frac{k}{y}>2k$  and  $\frac{k}{x}<2k$ .
Hence we arrive at our desired contradiction. Thus the two sequences are disjoint.  $\square$ Now we prove a few lemmas.**Lemma 1:** No two numbers in a sequence are equal.**Proof:** Suppose  $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$  and  $m>n$ . Let  $m=n+k$  for some  $k\in \mathbb{N}$ . Since  $x,y<1$ , we have  $\frac{k}{y}>k$  and  $\frac{k}{x}>k$ . Now  $\left\lfloor\frac{m}{y}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{n+k}{y}\right\rfloor\ge \left\lfloor\frac{n}{y}+k\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{y}\right\rfloor+k\ge \left\lfloor\frac{n}{y}\right\rfloor+1$ . Hence we can never have  $\left\lfloor\frac{n}{y}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{y}\right\rfloor$  if  $m\ne n$ .
An exact similar argument works for  $x$ .
This proves the lemma.  $\square$ **Lemma 2:** Any two consecutive numbers in the sequence  $(x_n)$  differ either by  $1$  or  $2$ .**Proof:** Note that since  $x>\frac{1}{2}$ , we have  $\left\lfloor\frac{m+1}{x}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{m}{x}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{x}+\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{m}{x}\right\rfloor\le \left\lfloor\frac{m}{x}+2\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{m}{x}\right\rfloor=2+\left\lfloor\frac{m}{x}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{m}{x}\right\rfloor=2$ .
So we are down with this lemma as well.  $\square$ Now with these tools ready, we proceed to kill the problem.
From our Lemma 2, we see that it is not possible for two consecutive natural numbers to be absent from the sequence  $(x_n)$ . Now consider any  $n\in\mathbb{N}$ . Suppose  $n\notin(x_n)$ . Then it follows that both  $n-1$  and  $n+1$  are in  $(x_n)$ . Let  $\left\lfloor\frac{m}{x}\right\rfloor=n-1$  and  $\left\lfloor\frac{m+1}{x}\right\rfloor=n+1$ .
From  $\left\lfloor\frac{m}{x}\right\rfloor=n-1$ , we get the inequality  $$ n-1<\frac{m}{x}<n $$  which after a little manipulation, resolves to  $$ \frac{n-m-1}{n-1}<1-x<\frac{n-m}{n} $$  giving us  $$ \frac{1}{1-x}=\frac{1}{y}>\frac{n}{n-m}. $$  Note that we do not have equality anywhere since  $x$  is irrational and a positive integer (rational number) can never equal an irrational one. (And I believe this is the only real significance of the irrationality of  $\alpha$  and  $\beta$  in this problem).

Similarly from  $\left\lfloor\frac{m+1}{x}\right\rfloor=n+1$ , we get  $$ n+1<\frac{m+1}{x}<n+2 $$  which turns into  $$ \frac{n-m}{n+1}<1-x<\frac{n-m+1}{n+2} $$  giving us  $$ \frac{1}{1-x}=\frac{1}{y}<\frac{n+1}{n-m}. $$  Hence we have  $n<\frac{n-m}{y}<n+1$ . Since  $\frac{m}{x}<n$  and  $x<1$ , we have  $m<nx<n$ , so  $n-m>0$ . Hence we see that  $\left\lfloor\frac{n-m}{y}\right\rfloor=n$ , which means that  $n\in (y_n)$ . Thus we have also proved that  $(x_n)\cup(y_n)=\mathbb{N}$ . Thus the problem has been solved.  $\blacksquare$</details>

stem_md: "Let  $\omega^3 = 1, \omega \neq 1$ . Show that $z_1, z_2, -\omega z_1, -\omega^2z_2$  are the vertices of an equilateral triangle."
solution_md: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. If the complex numbers $z_1, z_2, z_3$ are the vertices of an equilateral triangle, then \[\frac{z_3 - z_1}{z_2 - z_1} = \alpha = e^{\pm \pi i/3}.\]Hence $z_3 = (1 - \alpha) z_1 + \alpha z_2 = -\alpha^2 z_1 - \alpha^4 z_2,$ because $\alpha^2 - \alpha + 1 = 0$ and $\alpha^3 = - 1$ for either determination of $\alpha.$ Thus \[z_3 = -\omega z_1 - \omega^2 z_2\] where $\omega = \alpha^2 = e^{+2 \pi i / 3}$ is one of the two complex cube roots of unity. Note that given $z_1$ and $z_2$ there are two ways to complete an equilateral triangle, corresponding to the two choices for $\omega.$

stem_md: Let  $n$  be a positive integer. Prove that  $x^n -\frac{1}{x^{n}}$  is expressible as a polynomial in  $x-\frac{1}{x}$  with real coefficients if and only if  $n$  is odd.

stem_md: If  $f$  and  $g$  are real-valued functions of one real variable, show that there exist  $x$  and  $y$  in  $[0,1]$  such that   $$ |xy-f(x)-g(y)|\geq \frac{1}{4}. $$
solution_md:
Assume the contrary:  $|xy-f(x)-g(y)|<\dfrac{1}{4},\;\forall x,y\in[0,1]$ .
For  $x=y=0$  results:  $|f(0)+g(0)|<\dfrac{1}{4}\quad(1)$ .
For  $x=0,\,y=1$  results:  $|f(0)+g(1)|<\dfrac{1}{4}\quad(2)$ .
For  $x=1,\,y=0$  results:  $|f(1)+g(0)|<\dfrac{1}{4}\quad(3)$ .
For  $x=y=1$ , results  $|1-f(1)-g(1)|<\dfrac{1}{4}\Longrightarrow \dfrac{3}{4}<f(1)+g(1)<\dfrac{5}{4}\quad(4)$ .

Using  $(1),(2),(3)$  results: $|f(1)+g(1)|=|(f(1)+g(0))+(g(1)+f(0))-(f(0)+g(0))|\le|f(1)+g(0)|+|g(1)+f(0)|+|f(0)+g(0)|<\dfrac{3}{4}$ , contradiction with  $(4)$ .

Hence, the assumption  $|xy-f(x)-g(y)|<\dfrac{1}{4},\;\forall x,y\in[0,1]$  is false.
Results: exist at least a pair  $(x,y)\in[0,1]\times[0,1]$  such that  $|xy-f(x)-g(y)|\ge\dfrac{1}{4}$ .

stem_md: A sparrow, flying horizontally in a straight line, is  $50$  feet directly below an eagle and  $100$  feet directly above a hawk. Both hawk and eagle fly directly toward the sparrow, reaching it simultaneously. The hawk flies twice as fast as the sparrow. How far does each bird fly? At what rate does the eagle fly?
solution_md: Let $E, S, H$ denote the positions of the eagle, sparrow, and hawk respectively. Take the $x-$ axis vertical and the $y-$ axis horizontal, so that at $t = 0$ , the target is at $(0, 0)$ and the pursuer is at $(a, 0)$ . Assume the target ( $S$ ) has speed $v$ and the pursuer ( $E$ or $H$ ) has speed $kv$ with $k > 1$ . At time $t$ , the target is at $(0, vt)$ . The equations of motion are: $(dx/dt)^2 + (dy/dt)^2 = kv$ and $y' = (y - vt)/x$ . The first equation gives $\frac{kv}{dx/dt} = -\sqrt{1 + y'^{2}}$ (which is negative because $x$ decreases with time). Differentiating the second equation gives $xy'' = -\frac{v}{dx/dt}$ . So $kxy'' = \sqrt{1 + y'^{2}}$ . Integrating yields $\ln(y' + \sqrt{1 + y'^{2}} = \ln(x) + C$ . At $x = a, y = 0$ , so $(x/a)^{1/k} = y' + \sqrt{1 + y'^{2}}$ . Hence $2y' = (x/a)^{1/k} - (x/a)^{-1/k}$ . Integrating again yields $2y = \frac{a}{1+1/k} (x/a)^{1+1/k} - \frac{a}{1-1/k} (x/a)^{1-1/k} - \frac{a}{1+1/k} + \frac{a}{1-1/k}$ , since $y = 0$ at $x = a$ . When pursuit ends, $x = 0$ and hence $y = \frac{ak}{k^2 - 1}$ . For $H$ , we have $k = 2$ , so $y = 2a/3 = 200/3$ ft. That is, the distance travelled by $S$ . $H$ is travelling at twice the speed, so $B$ travels a distance $400/3$ ft. For $E$ reaches $S$ at the same $y$ , hence $200/3 = \frac{50k}{k^2 - 1}$ , so $4k^2 - 3k - 4 = 0$ , so $k = (3 + \sqrt{73})/8$ . Altogether, the answer includes: $E$ travels $\textcolor{red}{\frac{25(3 + \sqrt{73})}{3} = 96.2}$ ft, $H$ travels $\textcolor{red}{400/3 = 133.3}$ ft, $S$ travels $\textcolor{red}{200/3 = 66.7}$ ft, $E$ 's speed is $\textcolor{red}{\frac{3 + \sqrt{73}}{8} = 1.443}$ times T's speed.

stem_md:
Let  $m$  and  $n$  be integers greater than  $1$  and  $a_1 ,a_2 ,\ldots, a_{m+1}$  be real numbers. Prove that there exist real  $n\times n$  matrices  $A_1 ,A_2,\ldots, A_m$  such that 
(i)  $\det(A_j) =a_j$  for  $j=1,2,\ldots,m$  and
(ii)  $\det(A_1 +A_2 +\ldots+A_m)=a_{m+1}.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Choose   $$  A_1 = \begin{pmatrix}
a_1 & 0 & \cdots &0
t^2 & 1 & \cdots & 0
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots
0 &0& \cdot &1
\end{pmatrix}, \;\; A_2 = \begin{pmatrix}
a_2 & t& \cdots &0
0 & 1 & \cdots & 0
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots
0 &0& \cdot &1
\end{pmatrix} $$  for some  $t$  to be determined later. Furthermore, let  $A_i =\text{diag}(a_i , 1, 1 , \ldots, 1)$  for  $i>2.$  Then we see that condition (i) is fulfilled for all choices of  $t$  and  $$  \det(A_1 +A_2 +\cdots+A_m) = \det  \begin{pmatrix}
a_1+a_2 +\cdots+a_m & t & \cdots &0
t^2 & m & \cdots & 0
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots
0 &0& \cdot &m
\end{pmatrix} = -m^{n-2}t^3 +m^{n-1}(a_1 +a_2 +\ldots+a_m). $$  We can now choose  $t$  as a real root of the polynomial  $m^{n-2}X^3 -m^{n-1}(a_1 +a_2 +\cdots+a_m) +a_{m+1}$  and then condition (ii) holds, too.</details>

stem_md: Let each of  $m$  distinct points on the positive part of the  $x$ -axis be joined to  $n$  distinct points on the positive part of the  $y$ -axis. Obtain a formula for the number of intersection points of these segments, assuming that no three of the segments are concurrent.
solution_md:
The easy way: choose two x points and choose two y points to create two line segments which have one intersection. This gives us  $\dbinom{m}2\dbinom{n}2$  or  $\boxed{\dfrac{mn(m-1)(n-1)}{4}}$ .  $\square$ The other way: Start by joining each point  $x_i$  and one point  $y_1$ . The number of intersections on segment  $y_2x_2$  is  $m-1$ , and decreases by one until  $y_2x_m$  where there are no intersections. This gives us  $\sum_{i = 0}^{m-1} i = \dfrac{m(m-1)}{2}$  intersections for  $y_2$ . Applying the same logic for  $y_3$ , there are  $2(m-1)$  intersections on segment  $y_3x_2$ ,  $m-1$  contributed by  $y_1$  and another  $m-1$  contributed by  $y_2$ . The number of intersections decrease by 2 until  $y_3x_m$  where there are no intersections.

For each successive point, another factor is added onto  $(m-1)$  until  $y_nx_m$  where there are  $\dfrac{m(n-1)(m-1)}{2}$  intersections. This totals up to  $\left(\sum_{i = 0}^{n-1}i\right)\left(\dfrac{m(m-1)}2\right) = \boxed{\dfrac{mn(m-1)(n-1)}{4}}$ .  $\square$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/MAA AMC/Putnam/1959 Putnam/2864505.json

candidates: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. Each pair of points on the $X$ -axis together with each pair of points on the $Y$ -axis determine a convex quadrilateral whose diagonals meet somewhere in the first quadrant. Conversely, each intersection point arises in this way. Since no three segments are concurrent, except at the endpoints, each intersection point arises uniquely. There are, therefore, \[ \binom m2 \binom n2 = mn(m-1)(n-1) / 4\] points of intersection.

stem_md:
Given the following matrix  $$ \begin{pmatrix}
11& 17 & 25& 19& 16
24 &10 &13 & 15&3
12 &5 &14& 2&18
23 &4 &1 &8 &22 
6&20&7 &21&9
\end{pmatrix}, $$  choose five of these elements, no two from the same row or column, in such a way that the minimum of these elements is as large as possible.
solution_md:
We claim that the largest possible minimum is  $15$ , achievable by  $(23,20,25,15,18)$ . 

Suppose we could choose five of these elements, no two from the same row or column that are all greater than  $15$ . 

Note that we have to choose exactly one element from each row.

In the third row, the only number greater than  $15$  is  $18$  so we must choose that number. 

In the fourth row, the only number greater than  $15$  and not in the same column at  $18$  is  $23$ , so we must choose that number. 

In the second row, the only number greater than  $15$  is  $24$ , so we must choose that number. 

However,  $24$  and  $23$  are in the same column, contradiction.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/MAA AMC/Putnam/1959 Putnam/2864881.json

candidates:
The choice  $(25,15,18,23,20)$  shows that 15 can be attained. Suppose that all elements are  $>15$ .
Then we have 24 from the second row, 22 from the fourth row and we have no choices left for the third row.
This can also be seen by deleting the elements in  $[1,15]$ , listing the positions and trying to find a transversal.
Hence a minimum  $>15$  is not possible.

Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. Since the set of border elements of the matrix is the union of two rows and two columns, we may choose at most four elements from the border and must choose at least one element from the central $3 \times 3$ submatrix. Since the largest element in this central submatrix is $15,$ there is no admissible for which the minimum exceeds $15.$ But the choice $25, 15, 18, 23, 20$ satisfies the conditions and has minimum $15.$
Same solution as alexheinis.

stem_md:
For each positive integer  $n$ , let  $f_n$  be a real-valued symmetric function of  $n$  real variables. Suppose that for  all  $n$  and all real numbers  $x_1,\ldots,x_n, x_{n+1},y$  it is true that

  $\;(1)\; f_{n}(x_1 +y ,\ldots, x_n +y) = f_{n}(x_1 ,\ldots, x_n) +y,$   $\;(2)\;f_{n}(-x_1 ,\ldots, -x_n) =-f_{n}(x_1 ,\ldots, x_n),$   $\;(3)\; f_{n+1}(f_{n}(x_1,\ldots, x_n),\ldots, f_{n}(x_1,\ldots, x_n), x_{n+1}) =f_{n+1}(x_1 ,\ldots, x_{n}).$ Prove that  $f_{n}(x_{1},\ldots, x_n) =\frac{x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n}}{n}.$
solution_md:
For each positive integer $n$ , let $f_n$ be a real-valued symmetric function of $n$ real variables. Suppose that for all $n$ and all real numbers $x_1,\ldots,x_n, x_{n+1},y$ it is true that $\;(1)\; f_{n}(x_1 +y ,\ldots, x_n +y) = f_{n}(x_1 ,\ldots, x_n) +y,$ $\;(2)\;f_{n}(-x_1 ,\ldots, -x_n) =-f_{n}(x_1 ,\ldots, x_n),$ $\;(3)\; f_{n+1}(f_{n}(x_1,\ldots, x_n),\ldots, f_{n}(x_1,\ldots, x_n), x_{n+1}) =f_{n+1}(x_1 ,\ldots, x_{n}).$ Prove that $f_{n}(x_{1},\ldots, x_n) =\frac{x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n+1}}{n}.$
Let to be proved statement be the be S then for $n=1$ we have $f(x+y)=f(x)+y, f(-x)=-f(x)\implies f(0)=0$ putting $-x=y$ we get $f(0)=f(x)-x\implies f(x)=x$ So S is true for $n=1$ Assume S is true for some $n=k$ then we have $f_k(x_1,x_2,\cdots ,x_k)=\frac{x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_k}{k}$ Now we will prove that then it is also true for $n=k+1$ let $\{a_1,a_2,\cdots a_k\}, \{b_1,b_2,\cdots, b_k\}$ be 2 sets of $k$ real numbers such that $a-1+\cdots+a_k=b_1+\cdots+b_k$ then $f_k(a_1,a_2,\cdots a_k)=f_k(b_1,b_2,\cdots, b_k)\overset{\forall x\in R}{\implies} f_{k+1}(a_1,a_2,\cdots,a_k,x)=f_{k+1}(b_1,b_2,\cdots,b_k,x)\implies f_{k+1}(a_1,a_2,\cdots, a_k,-(a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_k))=f_{k+1}(0,0,\cdots,0,(a_1+a_2+\cdots a_k),-(a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_k))=0$ So $f_{k+1}(a_1+a_2+\cdots a_k,a_{k+1})=0$ if $a_1+\cdots a_{k+1}=0$ so $f(x_1-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K+1} x_i}{k+1},\cdots, x_{k+1}-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K+1} x_i}{k+1})=0=f_{k+1}(x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_{k+1})-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K+1} x_i}{k+1}$ hence if S is true for $n=k$ then it is also true for $n=k+1$ and it is already true for $n=1$ so by first pricipal of Mathematical induction we are done!

stem_md: Let  $n$  be a given positive integer. How many solutions are there in ordered positive integer pairs  $(x,y)$  to the equation  $$ \frac{xy}{x+y}=n? $$
solution_md: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. The given equation is equivalent to \[(x - n)(y - n) = n^2. \tag{1}\] Evidently, either both $x>n$ and $y>n,$ or $x 0,\,y - n > 0.$ It is clear that there are as many solutions as there are ordered factorizations of $n^2$ into two factors. If the prime factorization of $n$ is ${p_1}^{\alpha_1} {p_2}^{\alpha_2} \cdots {p_k}^{\alpha_k},$ then \[ n^2 = {p_1}^{2\alpha_1} {p_2}^{2\alpha_2} \cdots {p_k}^{2\alpha_k}\] and the number of ordered factorizations of $n^2$ is \[ (2\alpha_1 + 1)(2\alpha_2 + 1) \cdots (2\alpha_k + 1).\]
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/MAA AMC/Putnam/1960 Putnam/2861590.json

candidates:
Multiplying gives:  $\frac{xy}{x+y}=n \implies xy=n(x+y) \implies (x-n)(y-n) = n^2$ .

If both factors of positive, then we will have  $d(n^2)$  possible values. 

If both factors are negative, then at least one of the factors  $(x-n), (y-n)$  must be less than  $-n$ , but that contradicts the fact that  $x, y$  are positive integers. 

Thus we conclude the answer is  $d(n^2)$  where  $d(k)$  is the divisor function.

stem_md: Show that if  $t_1 , t_2, t_3, t_4, t_5$  are real numbers, then  $$ \sum_{j=1}^{5} (1-t_j )\exp \left( \sum_{k=1}^{j} t_k \right) \leq e^{e^{e^{e}}}. $$
solution_md:
Let  $f(t_1,...,t_5)=\sum_{j=1}^{5} (1-t_j )\exp \left( \sum_{k=1}^{j} t_k \right)=(1-t_1)e^{t_1}+(1-t_2)e^{t_1+t_2}+(1-t_3)e^{t_1+t_2+t_3}+(1-t_4)e^{t_1+t_2+t_3+t_4}+(1-t_5)e^{t_1+t_2+t_3+t_4+t_5}$ .
By also letting  $g(x)=(1-x)e^x$ , we get that  $g'(x)=-xe^x$  and thus the maximum of  $g$  over  $\mathbb R$  is attained at  $0$  and is worth  $1$ . 

Now, let  $\varphi_2(t_1,t_2)=(1-t_1)e^{t_1}+(1-t_2)e^{t_1+t_2}=e^{t_1}(1-t_1+(1-t_2)e^{t_2})$  and hence to maximize  $\varphi_2$  we must take  $t_2=0$ . Therefore to maximize  $\varphi_2$  we must maximize  $g_2(t_1)=\varphi_2(t_1,0)=(2-t_1)e^{t_1}$ . Again by differentiating, we find that the maximum of  $g_2$  is attained at  $t_1=1$  and is worth  $e$ .

Next we let  $\varphi_3(t_1,t_2,t_3)=(1-t_1)e^{t_1}+(1-t_2)e^{t_1+t_2}+(1-t_3)e^{t_1+t_2+t_3}=e^{t_1}(1-t_1+(1-t_2)e^{t_2}+(1-t_3)e^{t_2+t_3})$  which we can rewrite as  $\varphi_3(t_1,t_2,t_3)=e^{t_1}(1-t_1+\varphi_2(t_2,t_3))$  hence to maximize  $\varphi_3$  we must take  $t_2=1$  and  $t_3=0$  such that  $\varphi_2(t_2,t_3)=e$  and hence  $\varphi_3(t_1,t_2,t_3)=\varphi_3(t_1,1,0)=e^{t_1}(1-t_1+e)=g_3(t_1)$ . By differentiating  $g_3$ , we find that its maximum is attained at  $t_1=e$  and is worth  $e^e$ .

By repeating the exact same method  $2$  more times, we find that the maximum of  $f$  is attained at  $t_5=0, t_4=1, t_3=e, t_4=e^e, t_5=e^{e^e}$  and is worth  $e^{e^{e^{e}}}$  as wanted.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/MAA AMC/Putnam/1960 Putnam/2861597.json

candidates: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. We first show that \[\tag{1} (1 - s + a) e^s \le e^a\] for any choice of $s.$ The derivative of the function on the left with respect to $s$ is \[(a - s)e^s\] which vanishes only for $s = a,$ and this critical point is easily seen to be a maximum point, since $\lim_{s \to -\infty} (1 - s + a)e^s = 0$ and \[\lim_{s \to +\infty} (1 - s + a)e^s = - \infty.\] The claimed inequality $(1)$ follows. Then, taking $a = 0, s = t_5$ in $(1),$ we have \[ (1 - t_5 ) e^{t_5} \le e^0 = 1.\] Multiplying by the positive number $e^{t_4}$ and adding $(1 - t_4)e^{t_4},$ we find \[(1 - t_4) e^{t_4} + (1 - t_5) e^{t_4 + t_5} \le (1 - t_4)e^{t_4} + e^{t_4} \le e,\] the last step by $(1)$ with $a = 1.$ We continue this process. \[(1 - t_3) e^{t_3} + (1 - t_4) e^{t_3 + t_4} + (1 - t_5) e^{t_3+t_4+t_5}\le (1 - t_3) e^{t_3} + e \cdot e^{t_3} \le e^e.\] Similarly \begin{align*} (1 - t_2) e^{t_2} + (1 - t_3) e^{t_2 + t_3} + (1 - t_4) e^{t_2 + t_3 + t_4} &+ (1 - t_5) e^{t_2+t_3+t_4+t_5} & \le (1 - t_2) e^{t_2} + e^e e^{t_2} \le e^{e^e}\end{align*} and finally \[\sum^5_{j=1} (1 - t_j) \exp \left( \sum^j_{k=1} t_k \right) \le e^{e^{e^e}}.\]

stem_md:
Let  $N(n)$  denote the smallest positive integer  $N$  such that  $x^N =e$  for every element  $x$  of the symmetric group  $S_n$ , where  $e$  denotes the identity permutation. Prove that if  $n>1,$   $$ \frac{N(n)}{N(n-1)} =\begin{cases} p \;\text{if}\; n\; \text{is a power of a prime } p
1\; \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases} $$
solution_md: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. Let $L(n)$ be the least common multiple of the integers $1,2, \ldots, n.$ Then $L(n-1) \mid L(n)$ for $n = 2,3,\ldots .$ We shall prove that $N(n) = L(n)$ for all $n.$ In any group an element of order $i$ satisfies $x^N = e$ if and only if $i \mid N.$ Since the permutation group $\Sigma$ on $n$ symbols contains elements of each of the orders $1, 2, \ldots, n,$ we have $i \mid N(n)$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$ and therefore $L(n) \mid N(n).$ Conversely, every permutation in $\Sigma$ is the product of commuting cycles, each of which is of order at most $n,$ so $x^{L(n)} = e$ for all $x \in \Sigma.$ Hence $L(n) \ge N(n),$ and therefore $L(n) = N(n).$ Suppose $n$ is an integer greater than one but not a prime power. Then $n$ can be written as the product of two smaller integers that are relatively prime, say $n = ab.$ Then $a$ and $b$ both divide $L(n - 1).$ Since they are relatively prime, $ab = n$ also divides $L(n - 1).$ Therefore, $L(n) \mid L(n - 1)$ and hence $L(n) = L(n - 1)$ in this case. On the other hand, suppose $n$ is a power of a prime $p,$ say $n = p^{\alpha}.$ Then $n/p \mid L(n - 1),$ so $n \mid pL(n-1),$ and therefore $L(n) \mid pL(n-1).$ Now any integer less than $n$ is divisible by a power of $p$ no greater than $p^{\alpha - 1},$ so $p^\alpha \nmid L(n-1)$ and hence $L(n) \neq L(n-1).$ Thus $L(n) / L(n-1)$ divides $p,$ but $L(n) / L(n-1) \neq 1.$ Since $p$ is a prime, we have $L(n) / L(n-1) = p.$ in this case. Since $L(n) = N(n),$ we are done.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/MAA AMC/Putnam/1960 Putnam/2861609.json

stem_md: Evaluate the double series  $$ \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-3k -j -(k+j)^{2}}. $$
solution_md:
First, re-index and re-arrange (which is allowed since all terms are positive):  $$ \sum_{j=0}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-3k-j-(k+j)^2} = \sum_{j=0}^\infty \sum_{k=j}^\infty 2^{-3k+2j-k^2} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-3k-k^2} \sum_{j=0}^k 2^{2j} $$  Using the formula for a finite geometric series, we have  $$ \sum_{j=0}^k 2^{2j} = \frac{1}{3}\left(2^{2k+2} - 1\right), $$  so the original double series may be written as the single telescoping series  $$ \frac{1}{3} \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(2^{2-k-k^2} - 2^{-3k-k^2}\right) 
 = \frac{1}{3} \lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^N \left(2^{(1-k)(2+k)} - 2^{-k(3+k)}\right)  
 = \frac{1}{3} \lim_{N\to\infty} 2^{(1-0)(2+0)} - 2^{-N(3+N)}
 = \frac{4}{3} $$

stem_md: The motion of the particles of a fluid in the plane is specified by the following components of velocity  $$ \frac{dx}{dt}=y+2x(1-x^2 -y^2),\;\; \frac{dy}{dt}=-x. $$  Sketch the shape of the trajectories near the origin. Discuss what happens to an individual particle as  $t\to \infty$ , and justify your conclusion.
solution_md:
The key insight is that the unit circle  $x^2+y^2=1$  is one possible trajectory.  The velocity is  $(y + 2x - 2xr^2, - x) = (y, -x)$  on  $r = 1$ .   Hence, fluid starting inside this circle remains inside it and fluid starting outside it remains outside. Differentiating  $r^2 = x^2 + y^2$  gives  $r dr/dt = 2x^2(1 - r^2)$ . Hence if  $r < 1$ , then  $dr/dt > 0$ , so points inside the unit circle move outwards towards it. Similarly, if  $r > 1$ , then  $dr/dt < 0$ , so points outside the unit circle move inwards towards it.

To find the behavior close to the origin, we drop the cubic terms. The equations are then linear and can be solved to get  $x = (at + b)e^{t}, y = (-at + a - b)e^{t}$ . This gives S-shaped curves centered on the origin at a  $45^{\circ}$  angle touching the line  $y = -x$ .

stem_md: Consider the arithmetic progression  $a, a+d, a+2d,\ldots$  where  $a$  and  $d$  are positive integers. For any positive integer  $k$ , prove that the progression has either no  $k$ -th powers or infinitely many.
solution_md:
Suppose the sequence has a  $k$ th power.  Without loss of generality,  $a = b^k$  is a  $k$ th power, then as  $a > 0$ , without loss of generality,  $b > 0$ .

Then  $b+d > 0$  and   $$ (b+d)^k - b^k = ((b+d)-b)\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} (b+d)^ib^{k-1-i} = \left(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} (b+d)^ib^{k-1-i}\right)d $$  As  $n=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} (b+d)^ib^{k-1-i} > 0$  is a positive integer, we see that  $a + nd = (b+d)^k$  is a  $k$ th power.

By relabeling  $a+nd$  as  $a$  and repeating the argument, we find infinitely many  $k$ th powers.

stem_md: Any positive integer  $n$  can be written in the form  $n=2^{k}(2l+1)$  with  $k,l$  positive integers. Let  $a_n =e^{-k}$  and  $b_n = a_1 a_2 a_3 \cdots a_n.$  Prove that  $$ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n $$  converges.
solution_md:
Note that  $a_n=e^{-v_2(n)}$ . So  $b_n=e^{-\sum_{i=1}^n v_2(i)}$ Note that if  $n=2^k$ , then  $c_n=\sum_{i=1}^n v_2(i)$  follows the recurrence  $c_n=2c_{n/2}+1$ . Moreover, clearly  $c_n$  is a nondecreasing sequence since  $v_2(i)$  is nonnegative.
Consider the limit  $$ \lim_{k\to\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{2^k-1} b_n $$    $$ =\lim_{k\to\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{2^k-1} e^{-c_n} $$    $$ =\lim_{k\to\infty} \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\sum_{j=2^i}^{2^{i+1}-1} e^{-c_j} $$  Note that for  $2^{i-1}\leq j\leq 2^i-1$ ,  $c_j\geq c_{2^{i-1}}$ . So  $$ \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\sum_{j=2^i}^{2^{i+1}-1} e^{-c_j}\leq\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}2^i e^{-c_{2^i}} $$    $$ \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\sum_{j=2^i}^{2^{i+1}-1} e^{-c_j}\leq\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{1}{e^{c_{2^i}-i\ln 2}} $$  We can solve explicitly for  $c_{2^i}$  to see that  $c_{2^i}=2^i-1$ , hence  $$ \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\sum_{j=2^i}^{2^{i+1}-1} e^{-c_j}\leq\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{1}{e^{2^i-1-i\ln 2}} $$  Clearly, for sufficiently large  $i$ ,  $2^i-1-i\ln 2\geq i$ , so since  $$ \lim_{k\to\infty} \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \frac{1}{e^i} $$  converges. We know by comparison test that  $\lim_{k\to\infty} \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\sum_{j=2^i}^{2^{i+1}-1} e^{-c_j}$  converges.

stem_md: Find all integer solutions  $(m,n)$  to  $m^{n}=n^{m}.$
solution_md:
Notice that both are negative or positive, so WLOG consider them positive. Also,  $n=m$  trivially works, so consider  $n \neq m$ . $m^n=n^m \Rightarrow n \cdot ln(m)=m \cdot ln(n) \Rightarrow \frac{n}{ln(n)}=\frac{m}{ln(m)}$ . Considering the function  $f(x)=\frac{x}{ln(x)}$ , we can check:
-Continuous because  $x$  and  $ln(x)$  are continuous.
- $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0^+}f(x)=\frac{0}{-\infty}=0$ ,  $\lim_{x \rightarrow 1^-}f(x)=-\frac{1}{0}=-\infty$ ,  $\lim_{x \rightarrow 1^+}f(x)=\frac{1}{0}=\infty$ ,  $\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty}f(x)=\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{x^{-1}}=\infty$  (L'hoppital last one).
- $f(x) \frac{d}{dx}=\frac{ln(x)-1}{ln^2(x)}=0 \Leftrightarrow x=e$ . As  $ln^2(x)>0$ , we know that  $f(x)$  decreases on  $(0,1) \cup (1,e)$  and increases on  $(e, \infty)$ .
We need two positive integers  $n \neq m$  such  $f(n)=f(m)$ . From the previous information,  $f$  isn't inyective on  $(1, \infty)$ , with  $e$  as it minimum. The unique integer in  $(1, e)$  is  $2$ . There is only one integer that  $f(2)=f(b)$ , and it's easy to see that is  $4$ .
We conclude that the possible answers are  $(m, n)=(a, a); (-a, -a); (2, 4); (4, 2)$  where  $a \in \mathbb{Z^+}$  $a^a=a^a, -a^{-a}=-a^{-a}, 2^4=16=4^2$

stem_md: Let  $g(t)$  and  $h(t)$  be real, continuous functions for  $t\geq 0.$  Show that any function  $v(t)$  satisfying the differential inequality  $$ \frac{dv}{dt}+g(t)v \geq h(t),\;\; v(t)=c, $$  satisfies the further inequality  $v(t)\geq u(t),$  where   $$ \frac{du}{dt}+g(t)u = h(t),\;\; u(t)=c. $$  From this, conclude that for sufficiently small  $t>0,$  the solution of  $$ \frac{dv}{dt}+g(t)v = v^2 ,\;\; v(t)=c $$  may be written  $$ v=\max_{w(t)} \left( c e^{- \int_{0}^{t} |g(s)-2w(s)| \, ds} -\int_{0}^{t} e^{-\int_{0}^{t} |g(s')-2w(s')| \, ds'} w(s)^{2} ds \right), $$  where the maximum is over all continuous functions  $w(t)$  defined over some  $t$ -interval  $[0,t_0 ].$
solution_md:
Let us take  $F(x) = \int_{0}^{x} f(t) dt$  and put  $A(x) = a(x)e^{F(x)}, B(x) = b(x)e^{F(x)}$ . Then: $A' = (a' + f a) e^{F} = g e^{F}$ ; $B' = (b' + f b) e^{F} \ge g e^{F}$ ;

since  $e^{F} > 0$ . Hence  $B' \ge A'$  for all  $x$ . But  $B(0) = A(0) \Rightarrow B(x) \ge A(x)$  for all  $x \Rightarrow$  hence  $b(x) \ge a(x)$  for all  $x$ .

Let  $u$  be any continuous function on  $\mathbb{R}$ . Put  $U(x) = \int_{0}^{x} u(t) dt$  and put  $h(x) = F(x) - 2 U(x) = \int_{0}^{x} f(t) - 2u(t) dt$ . Then  $h(0) = 0$ . We have  $(y - u)^{2} \ge 0$ , so  $y^{2} - 2uy \ge -u^{2}$ . Now put  $z = ye^{h}$ , so that  $z(0) = y(0) e^{h(0)} = d$ .

From there,  $z' = (y' + h'y) e^{h} = (y' + (f - 2u)y) e^{h} = (y^2 - 2uy) e^{h} \ge -u^{2} e^{h}$ . Hence  $z(x) = z(0) + \int_{0}^{x} z'(t) dt\ge d - \int_{0}^{x} u(t)^2 e^{h(t)} dt$ . Hence  $y(x) = z(x) e^{-h(x)} \ge d e^{-h(x)} - \int_{0}^{x} e^{-[h(x) - h(t)]} u(t)^2 dt$ . So  $z(x) \ge$  the maximum over all  $u$ .  If we put  $u = y$  (the solution), then we get equality.

stem_md: For a real-valued function  $f(x,y)$  of two positive real variables  $x$  and  $y$ , define  $f$  to be *linearly bounded* if and only if there exists a positive number  $K$  such that  $|f(x,y)| < K(x+y)$  for all positive  $x$  and  $y.$  Find necessary and sufficient conditions on the real numbers  $\alpha$  and  $\beta$  such that  $x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}$  is linearly bounded.
solution_md:
Suppose  $x^\alpha y^\beta$  is linearly bounded.
If  $\alpha+\beta>1$ , consider  $x=y\to \infty$ . Contradiction!
If  $\alpha+\beta<1$ , consider  $x=y\to 0$ . Contradiction!
If  $\alpha<0$ , consider  $x\to 0, y=1$ . Contradiction!
If  $\beta<0$ , consider  $y\to 0, x=1$ . Contradiction!
If  $\alpha + \beta=1$ ,  $\alpha,\beta \geq 0$ , then  $x^\alpha y^\beta \leq \alpha x + \beta y$  by Young's inequality.
Answer:  $\boxed{\alpha + \beta=1, \alpha,\beta \geq 0}$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/MAA AMC/Putnam/1961 Putnam/2857956.json

Suppose $x^\alpha y^\beta < K(x+ y)$ for all positive $x, y.$ Setting $x = y= t,$ we find $t^{\alpha+\beta-1} < 2K$ for all positive $t.$ It follows that $\alpha + \beta = 1.$ Now set $x = s, y = 1-s.$ Then $s^\alpha (1 - s)^\beta < K$ for $0 < s < 1.$ Letting $s \to 0,$ we see that $\alpha \ge 0.$ Letting $s \to 1,$ we find $\beta \ge 0.$ Thus, in order that $x^\alpha y^\beta$ be linearly bounded, it is necessary that $\alpha \ge 0, \beta \ge 0,$ and $\alpha + \beta = 1.$ Conversely, suppose $\alpha \ge 0, \beta \ge 0, \alpha + \beta =1.$ Then for $0 < t < 1,$ it is obvious that \[ t^\alpha (1 - t)^\beta < 1^\alpha \cdot 1^\beta =1.\] Hence \[x^\alpha y^\beta = \left( \frac x{x + y} \right)^\alpha \left(1 - \frac x{x +y}\right)^\beta (x + y) < x + y\] for any positive $x$ and $y,$ so $x^\alpha y^\beta$ is linearly bounded with $K = 1.$ Thus the conditions stated are both necessary and sufficient.

stem_md: Let  $\Omega(n)$  be the number of prime factors of  $n$ . Define  $f(1)=1$  and  $f(n)=(-1)^{\Omega(n)}.$  Furthermore, let   $$ F(n)=\sum_{d|n} f(d). $$  Prove that  $F(n)=0,1$  for all positive integers  $n$ . For which integers  $n$  is  $F(n)=1?$
solution_md:
The function  $f$  is multiplicative and so is  $F$ , by standard properties of Dirichlet convolution.
Hence it suffices to check  $F(p^k)$  for  $p$  a prime.
But
\[F(p^k)=\sum_{j=0}^k f(p^j)=\sum_{j=0}^k (-1)^j\]
which is  $0$  if  $k$  is odd and  $1$  if  $k$  is even.
The claim follows and we see that  $F(n)=1$  iff  $n$  is a perfect square.

stem_md: Let  $S$  be a nonempty closed set in the euclidean plane for which there is a closed disk  $D$  containing  $S$  such that  $D$  is a subset of every closed disk that contains  $S$ . Prove that every point inside  $D$  is the midpoint of a segment joining two points of  $S.$
solution_md:
We prove that all points on the boundary  $\partial D$  of the disk belong to  $S$ . Let  $x\in \partial D$ . Assume for the sake of contradiction  $x\notin S$ . Since  $S$  is closed, there exists a disk  $D(x,\varepsilon)$  centered at  $x$  with radius  $\varepsilon>0$  that is free of points of  $S$ . Let  $x_1,x_2$  be the two points at which the circle  $\partial D$  meets the circle  $\partial D(x,\varepsilon)$ . Note that  $S$  is in one of the half-planes determined by the line  $x_1x_2$ . This means there exists a circle through  $x_1$  and  $x_2$  with sufficiently large radius that contains  $S$ . But it does not contain  $D$ , since  $x$  is outside that circle, contradiction.
 Hence,  $\partial D\subset S$  and the result follows.

stem_md: Let  $a$  and  $b$  be given positive real numbers, with  $a<b.$  If two points are selected at random from a straight line segment of length  $b,$  what is the probability that the distance between them is at least  $a?$
solution_md: Solution : Consider which points (x,y) of the square x=0 to b, y=0 to b have |x-y| greater than or equal to a. Evidently the acceptable points lie in the two right angled triangles : (0,a), (0,b), (b-a,b), and (a,0), (b,0), (b,b-a). These fit together to give a square side b-a, so the area of the acceptable points is  $(b-a)^2$  out of a total area of  $b^2$ . Thus the probability is ( $(b-a)^2$ )/ $b^2$  .

stem_md: Assume that  $|f(x)|\leq 1$  and  $|f''(x)|\leq 1$  for all  $x$  on an interval of length at least  $2.$  Show that  $|f'(x)|\leq 2 $  on the interval.
solution_md:
Take the interval to be  $[-1, 1]$ . Taylor's formula gives:
\[
f(1) = f(x) + (1 - x) f'(x) + \frac{(1 - x)^2}{2} f''(h),
\]
\[
f(-1) = f(x) + (-1 - x) f'(x) + \frac{(-1 - x)^2}{2} f''(k),
\]
for some  $h, k \in [-1, 1]$ .

Subtracting, we have:
\[
f(1) - f(-1) = 2 f'(x) + \frac{(1 - x)^2}{2} f''(h) - \frac{(1 + x)^2}{2} f''(k).
\]

Taking absolute values:
\[
2 |f'(x)| \leq |f(1)| + |f(-1)| + \frac{(1 - x)^2}{2} |f''(h)| + \frac{(1 + x)^2}{2} |f''(k)|.
\]

Since  $|f(1)| \leq 1$ ,  $|f(-1)| \leq 1$ ,  $|f''(h)| \leq 1$ , and  $|f''(k)| \leq 1$ , we have:
\[
2 |f'(x)| \leq 2 + \frac{(1 - x)^2}{2} + \frac{(1 + x)^2}{2}.
\]

Simplifying:
\[
2 |f'(x)| \leq 2 + \frac{1 - 2x + x^2}{2} + \frac{1 + 2x + x^2}{2} = 2 + \frac{2 + 2x^2}{2} = 3 + x^2.
\]

Since  $x^2 \leq 1$ , we have:
\[
2 |f'(x)| \leq 4 \implies |f'(x)| \leq 2.
\]

<details><summary>solution</summary>1.  $0 \not\in S$ , since if  $0 \in S$ , this would contradict the second property when  $r=0$ .
2. For every positive rational number  $r$ , either  $r \in S$  or  $-r \in S$  but not both (by the second property).

6. Lastly, since no negative rational number is in  $S$ , statement 2. implies every positive rational number is in  $S$ .

stem_md: Let  $x^{(n)}=x(x-1)\cdots (x-n+1)$  for  $n$  a positive integer and let  $x^{(0)}=1.$  Prove that  $$ (x+y)^{(n)}= \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} x^{(k)} y^{(n-k)}. $$
solution_md:
Why does it suffice to show that it holds for nonnegative integers?
Essentially if a polynomial $p(x,y) \in \mathbf{C}[x,y]$ vanishes on a large enough rectangle, then it must be the zero polynomial. Suppose we know that $p(a,b) = 0$ for all positive integers $a,b$ . We can think of $p(x,y)$ as a polynomial in $y$ with coefficients in $\mathbf{C}[x]$ and write $p(x,y) = \sum_{i=0}^m p_i(x)y^i$ . By assumption, the polynomial $p(a,y) = \sum_{i=0}^m p_i(a)y^i \in \mathbf{C}[y]$ has infinitely many roots for all positive integers $a$ , so $p(a,y)$ must be the zero polynomial for all such $a$ . This means that $p_i(x)$ has infinitely many roots for all $i=1,\ldots,m$ . So each $p_i(x)$ is also the zero polynomial. Hence $p(x,y) = 0$ , as claimed. Now apply this result to the polynomial $p(x,y) = (x+y)^{(n)} - \sum_k \tbinom{n}{k} x^{(k)} y^{(n-k)}$ . The principle outlined above can be generalized to polynomials in more variables. Also the size of the rectangle on which the polynomial must vanish can be reduced significantly.

stem_md: Prove that for every integer  $n$  greater than  $1:$   $$ \frac{3n+1}{2n+2} < \left( \frac{1}{n} \right)^{n} + \left( \frac{2}{n} \right)^{n}+ \ldots+\left( \frac{n}{n} \right)^{n} <2. $$
solution_md:
Suppose  $m \le n$ .  By expanding by the binomial theorem, we obtain: $mn = [(m-1) + 1]^n = (m-1)^n + n(m-1)^{n-1} +$  additional positive terms  $> (m-1)^n + n(m-1)^{n-1} > 2 (m-1)^n$ . 

Hence,  $n^n > (n-1)^n + (n-1)^n > (n-1)^n + (n-2)^n + (n-2)^n > ... > (n-1)^n + (n-2)^n + ... + 1^n$ . So  $2n^n > \sum_{k=1}^{n} r^n$ , which is one of the two required inequalities.

The other case is slightly harder. We approximate the integral of  $f(x) = x^n$  between  $0$  and  $1$ . We have to do slightly better than the usual Riemann sums. We also take into account the small triangles. The curve has increasing gradient, so the area under the curve between  $(r-1)/n$  and  $r/n$  is less than the area under the chord joining  $( (r-1)/n, f( (r-1)/n ) )$  and  $(r/n, f(r/n) )$ . Summing those areas gives:  $(1/n) \sum_{k=1}^{n} (r/n)^n - (1/2n)\sum_{k=1}^{n} ( (r/n)n - ( (r-1)/n )^n = (1/n)K - (1/2n) (n/n)^n$ , where  $K = \sum_{k=1}^{n} (r/n)^n$ . The integral is just  $1/(n+1)$ , so we have:  $1/(n+1) < K/n - 1/(2n) \Rightarrow K > n/(n+1) + 1/2 = (3n+1)/(2n+2)$ .

Hence \[\frac 1{n + 1} = \int^1_0 x^n\,\mathrm dx < \frac 1n \left[ \frac 12 \left( \frac 0n \right)^n + \left( \frac 1n \right)^n + \left (\frac 2n \right)^n + \cdots + \left(\frac {n-1}n \right)^n + \frac 12 \left(\frac nn \right)^n \right].\] Multiply by $n$ and add $1/2$ to get \[\frac {3n + 1}{2n + 2} = \frac n{n + 1} + \frac 12 < \left[ \left( \frac 1n \right)^n + \left(\frac 2n \right)^n + \cdots + \left(\frac{n-1}n \right)^n + \left(\frac nn \right)^n \right].\] The required upper approximation can be obtained by considering the lower Riemann sum over the same subdivision (and adding $1$ to both sides), but the argument below gives a much sharper estimate. Since $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for any $x,$ we have \[\left(1 - \frac in \right)^n \le e^{-i}\] for $0 \le i \le n.$ Hence \begin{align*} \left( \frac nn \right)^n + \left(\frac{n-1}n \right)^n + \cdots + \left(\frac 2n \right)^n + \left( \frac 1n \right)^n & \le 1 + e^{-1} + \cdots + e^{-(n-1)} & \le \frac 1{1 - e^{-1}} = \frac e{e - 1} < 2.\end{align*} Since $\lim_{n \to \infty} (1 - i/n)^n = e^{-i},$ it follows easily that \[\lim_{n \to \infty} \left[ \left(\frac nn \right)^n + \left(\frac {n-1}n \right)^n + \cdots + \left(\frac 2n \right)^n + \left( \frac 1n \right)^n \right] = \frac e{e -1 }.\]

stem_md: Let  $f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$  be a strictly increasing function such that  $f(2)=2$  and  $f(mn)=f(m)f(n)$ for every pair of relatively prime positive integers  $m$  and  $n$ . Prove that  $f(n)=n$  for every positive integer  $n$ .
solution_md:
Let $f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ be a strictly increasing function such that $f(2)=2$ and $f(mn)=f(m)f(n)$ for every pair of relatively prime positive integers $m$ and $n$ . Prove that $f(n)=n$ for every positive integer $n$ .
It's obvious to see that $f(1)=1$ , now we will exploit the multiplicative condition of $f$ . For any odd $n$ , $f(2n)=f(2).f(n)=2f(n)$ . We prove a claim now which basically does all the work.**Claim:** $f(3)=3$ Let $f(3)=k$ , then $f(6)=2k\implies k+2\le f(5)\le 2k-1$ otherwise $4$ will have no place to map onto. This further implies $f(10)\le 4k-2\implies f(9)\le 4k-3\implies f(18)\le 8k-6\implies f(15)\le 8k-9$ . Now $f(15)=f(3).f(5)\ge k(k+2)$ . Therefore combining both the inequalities we get $$ k(k+2)\le f(15)\le 8k-9\implies(k-3)^2\le 0\implies k\le 3 $$ Clearly $k<3$ is not possible because of the monotonicity condition, therefore $k=3$ . $\square$ Now it's immediate to see why $f(n)=n$ . We use the following well known
LemmaIf $f:S\to S$ , where $S\subset\mathbb{N}$ is an order preserving bijection, then $f$ is the identity on $S$ .
. We can write $$ \mathbb{N}=\{1,2\}\cup\{3,\cdots, 6\}\cup\{5,\cdots 10\}\cup\{9,\cdots,18\}\cdots(\bigstar) $$ From the **Claim** above $f$ fixes $3$ , thus fixes $6$ , too, so from the
LemmaIf $f:S\to S$ , where $S\subset\mathbb{N}$ is an order preserving bijection, then $f$ is the identity on $S$ .
, it fixes $\{3,4,5,6\}$ , again from a similar reasoning we get $f$ fixes $\{5,\cdots,10\}$ , and so on, therefore from $(\bigstar)$ we get $f$ fixes $\mathbb{N}$ . $\blacksquare$
Some MotivationThe part after the claim is very easy to see (because if it fixes 3, it will fix 6, so it will fix everything in between 3 and 6, in particular 5, so it will also fix everything 5 and 10 and this process will go on.), so just proving that $f$ fixes $3$ , should do the job, assign $f(3)=k$ , which gives you $f(6)=2k$ , certainly you don't get any more equalities to work with, but because of the strict monotonicity condition, you do get some inequalities. Giving upper bounds and lower bounds to certain $f(n)$ 's and combining them the right way gives you some inequality on $k$ , where from it's easy to extract the possible values of $k$ . This kind of hits home the fact that if you don't have equalities, try find some inequalities instead and work with them.

stem_md: Find an integral formula for the solution of the differential equation  $$ \delta (\delta-1)(\delta-2) \cdots(\delta -n +1) y= f(x), \;\;\, x\geq 1, $$  for  $y$  as a function of  $f$  satisfying the initial conditions  $y(1)=y'(1)=\ldots= y^{(n-1)}(1)=0$ , where  $f$  is continuous and  $\delta$  is  the differential operator  $ x \frac{d}{dx}.$
solution_md:
Let  $E = \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(\delta-k)$ .  The first step is to try to simplify  $Ey$ , which after experimenting with small  $n$  we soon find that  $Ey = x^{n+1}y^{(n+1)}$  (which is easily proved via induction).

Therefore, we seek a solution to  $x^{n+1}y^{(n+1)} = f(x)$ , subject to  $y(1) = y'(1) = ... = y^{(n)}(1) = 0$ .  The trick is to use the Taylor expansion:  $\textcolor{red}{y(x) = y(1) + (x-1)y'(1) + \frac{(x-1)^2}{2!} y''(1) + ... + (x-1)^{n}y^{(n)}(1) + \int_{1}^{x} g(t) dt}$ , 

where  $g(t) = \frac{(x - t)^{n}y^{n+1}(t)}{n!} = \frac{(x - t)^{n}f(t)}{n! t^{n+1}}$ .

stem_md: i) Prove that if a function  $f$  is continuous on the closed interval  $[0, \pi]$  and   $$  \int_{0}^{\pi} f(t) \cos t \; dt=  \int_{0}^{\pi} f(t) \sin t \; dt=0, $$  then there exist points  $0 < \alpha < \beta < \pi$  such that  $f(\alpha) =f(\beta) =0.$ ii) Let  $R$  be a bounded, convex, and open region in the Euclidean plane. Prove with the help of i) that the centroid of  $R$    bisects at least three different chords of the boundary of  $ R.$
solution_md:
Now for the ii).

Moar facts:

Fact 3: any antiperiodic continuous function of period  $p$ , that is  $f(x+p)=-f(x)$  (like sine and cosine) has at least two roots in  $[0,2p[$ -
Proof: note that if  $r$  is a root of  $f$  then  $f(r+kp)=0$  for any  $k$  integer. So if  $f(0)=0$  we are done. if  $f(0)\neq 0$  then Bolzano in  $[0,p]$  and hence in  $[p,2p]$ .

Fact 4: any product of two antiperiodic functions of period  $p$  is periodic of period  $p$ . (like signs)
Proof:  $f(x+p)g(x+p)=-f(x)\times -g(x)=f(x)g(x)$ . Done.

Fact 5: any periodic integrable function  $f$  of period  $p$  satisfies the property:  $\int_0^p f(x)dx=\int_c^{p+c}f(x)dx$  for any real  $c$ .
Proof: DIY

Fact 6: for any antiperiodic  $f$  continuous function of period  $\pi$  satisfying (C) and (S) then  $f(x+c)$  also satisfies (C) and (S) for any  $c$ Proof: By Fact 4 (and the comment of Fact 3)  $f(x)\sin x$  and  $f(x)\cos x$  are periodic of period  $\pi$ , now by Fact 2, change of variables and Fact 5:  $$ 0=\int_0^{\pi} f(x)\sin(x+a)dx=\int_{a}^{\pi+a} f(x-a)\sin x dx=^{(F5)} \int_0^{\pi} f(x-a)\sin x dx $$  Now put  $c=-a$ . QED.
----------------------------------------------------------------

Intermediate result 1 1/2:

If  $f$  is an antiperiodic function of period  $p$  that satisfies the conditions in (i) (yea you would think this is frickin annoying to say this) then there is at least three roots in  $[0,\pi[$ .

Proof: By Fact 6, any shifting in  $f$  meets the conditions (C) and (S) and by Fact 3 we can choose the function  $f(x+r)$  with  $r$  a root of  $f$ . So applying (i) to  $f(x+r)$  we can have at least two roots in  $]0,\pi[$  and by counting the root in the beggining, we have at least three roots in  $[0,\pi[$ .

--------------------------------------------------------------
Proof of (ii):

We know that the centroid is given (in double integrals as)   $$ \bar{x}=\dfrac{1}{A(R)}\iint_R xdA, \bar{y}=\dfrac{1}{A(R)}\iint_R ydA,A(R)=\iint_R dA $$  Now we put a translated polar coordinates giving by  $x-\bar{x}=r\cos \theta$  and  $y-\bar{y}=r\sin \theta, r>0,\theta \in [0,2\pi[$ . By definition of centroid, we always have:  $$ \iint_R (x-\bar{x})dA=\iint_R{y-\bar{y}}dA=0 $$   (Now is gonna looks like the conditions in (i))
And we remember that using transformation theorem we have  $dA=rdrd\theta$ . Now in polar coordinates looks like:  $$ \iint_R r^2 \cos \theta drd\theta=\iint_R r^2 \sin \theta drd\theta=0 $$  We then define  $r=f(\theta)$  as a function that measures the distance of the centroid to the boundary. So why we need a convex set, basically because:

1) any chord in the boundary (except the extremes) belongs to the set
2) the centroid belongs to  $R$ .
3) the function  $f(\theta)$  is forced to be continuous (needs more details)

Now:  $$ \iint_R r^2\cos \theta drd\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{f(\theta)} r^2\cos \theta drd\theta=\int_0^{2\pi} \dfrac{1}{3}f(\theta)^3 \cos \theta d\theta=0 $$  and similarily:  $$ \iint_R r^2\sin \theta drd\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{f(\theta)} r^2\cos \theta drd\theta=\int_0^{2\pi} \dfrac{1}{3}f(\theta)^3 \sin \theta d\theta=0 $$  This implies  $\int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta)^3 \cos \theta d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta)^3 \sin \theta d\theta=0$ , now partitioning:  $$ \int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta)^3 \cos \theta d\theta=\int_0^{\pi} f(\theta)^3 \cos \theta d\theta+\int_\pi^{2\pi} f(\theta)^3 \cos \theta d\theta=0 $$    $$ \int_0^{\pi} f(\theta)^3 \cos \theta d\theta+\int_0^{\pi} f(\theta+\pi)^3 \cos (\theta+\pi) d\theta=0 $$    $$ \int_0^{\pi} f(\theta)^3 \cos \theta d\theta-\int_0^{\pi} f(\theta+\pi)^3 \cos (\theta) d\theta=0 $$    $$ \int_0^{\pi}(f(\theta)^3 -f(\theta+\pi)^3) \cos (\theta) d\theta=0 $$  And therefore, in similar way that i don't wanna do:  $$ \int_0^{\pi}(f(\theta)^3 -f(\theta+\pi)^3) \sin (\theta) d\theta=0 $$  This implies  $g(\theta)=f(\theta)^3 -f(\theta+\pi)^3$  satisfies the conditions in (i). Note that if  $\theta_0$  is a root of  $g$ , then  $f(\theta_0)=f(\theta_0+\pi)$ , meaning, that the coord that passes thru one extreme to another containing the centroid, is bisected by the same centroid. But, there is more. we note that  $g(\theta+\pi)=f(\theta+\pi)^3 -f(\theta)^3=-g(\theta)$  so is antiperiodic of period  $2\pi$ .
Now, by the intermediate result, we have at least three roots of  $g$ , meaning at least three values of  $\theta \in [0,\pi]$ , therefore, there are at least three coords that the centroid bisects.

Regards
Claudio.

Proof: By contradiction and Bolzano. 

Fact 2: If (C) and (S) holds, then  $\int_0^{\pi} f(x)\sin(x+a)dx=0$  for all  $a \in \mathbb{R}$ .
Proof: Oh god please.... DIY

-------------------------------------------------------
Now the proof. Suppouse  $f$  continuous in  $[0,\pi]$  satisfies (C) and (S):

Part 1: there is at least one change of sign in  $]0,\pi[$  and hence, exists  $c \in ]0,\pi[$  such that  $f(c)=0$ .

stem_md: For what integers  $a$  does  $x^2 -x+a$  divide  $x^{13}+ x +90$  ?
solution_md:
Let  $x=0$ . Then,  $a|90$ .
Let  $x=1$ . Then,  $a|92$ .
From the above, the possible values of  $a$  is  $\pm1$  or  $\pm2$ . Since  $f(x)=x^{13}+x+90$  only has one real solutions,  $g(x)=x^2-x+a$  has at most  $1$  real solution. So,  $a>0$ .
If  $a=1$ , then  $\omega^3=-1$ , where  $\omega$  is a non-real solution to  $g(x)=0$ . But,  $f(\omega)=\omega+\omega+90\neq0$ . So,  $a\neq1$ .
If  $a=2$ , then you can check by the long division or something.
