For what it's worth, here is my proposed solution of the even case; its main advantage at this point is dealing with the  $n \equiv 2 \mod 4$  case without cycle hacking.

<details><summary>Mostly direct copypaste from problem submission</summary>\textbf{Problem.} Let  $n$  be an even positive integer. Consider the following statement:

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(A)] For each integer  $a$  coprime to  $n$ , there exists a permutation  $\pi$  of  $\left\{  1,2,\ldots,n\right\}  $  such that  $\pi\left(  \pi\left( x\right)  \right)  \equiv ax$  for each  $x\in\left\{  1,2,\ldots,n\right\}  $ .
\end{enumerate}

Prove that (A) holds if and only if  $4\nmid n$ .

\textbf{Remark.}
If  $n$  is odd (as opposed to even), statement (A) never holds [UPDATE: I forgot to say "unless  $n=1$ "]. This could be added to the problem, but my proof is nowhere as nice as the above argument for the even- $n$  case. (If an odd  $n$  has prime factorization  $p_{1}^{a_{1}}p_{2}^{a_{2}}\cdots p_{k}^{a_{k}}$ , then we can pick a primitive root  $g$  modulo  $p_{1}^{a_{1}}$ , and then multiplication by  $g$  does not act on  $\mathbb{Z}/n$  as the square of a permutation, because it has an odd number of cycles of length  $p_{1}^{a_{1}}-p_{1}^{a_{1}-1}$ .)

\textbf{Remark.}
This problem was inspired by quadratic reciprocity and some variations, particularly the one in:

\href{https://doi.org/10.1080/00029890.2005.11920190}{William Duke, Kimberly Hopkins, \textit{Quadratic Reciprocity in a Finite Group}, American Mathematical Monthly \textbf{112}:3, 251-256.}

But I don't know whether it follows from or implies anything in the literature.

\textbf{Solution to the problem (sketched).}

Let  $\mathbb{Z}/n =\left\{  \overline{0},\overline{1},\overline{2},\ldots,\overline{n-1}\right\}  $  denote the additive group of residue classes of integers modulo  $n$ . Then, by replacing the numbers  $1,2,\ldots,n$  by their residue classes, we can rewrite statement (A) as follows:

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(B)] For each integer  $a$  coprime to  $n$ , there exists a permutation  $\pi$  of  $\mathbb{Z}/n$  such that  $\pi\left(  \pi\left(  x\right)  \right) =ax$  for each  $x\in\mathbb{Z}/n$ .
\end{enumerate}

So statement (A) is equivalent to statement (B). Thus, it remains to prove that this statement (B) holds if and only if  $4\nmid n$ .

We shall prove the `` $\Longrightarrow$ '' and `` $\Longleftarrow$ '' directions of this equivalence separately: $\Longrightarrow:$  Assume that (B) holds. We must prove that  $4\nmid n$ .

Apply statement (B) to  $a=-1$ . Thus, we see that there exists a permutation  $\pi$  of  $\mathbb{Z}/n$  such that  $\pi\left(  \pi\left(  x\right)  \right) =\left(  -1\right)  x$  for each  $x\in\mathbb{Z}/n$ . In other words, multiplication by  $-1$  on  $\mathbb{Z}/n$  (regarded as a permutation of  $\mathbb{Z}/n$ ) is the square of a permutation. In particular, multiplication by  $-1$  on  $\mathbb{Z}/n$  is an even permutation of  $\mathbb{Z}/n$  (since the square of any permutation is an even permutation). But this permutation is a composition of  $n/2-1$  transpositions (indeed, it is explicitly given as  $\underbrace{\left(  \overline{1},\overline{n-1}\right)  \left(  \overline{2},\overline{n-2}\right)  \cdots\left(  \overline{n/2-1},\overline{n/2+1}\right)  }_{n/2-1\text{ transpositions}}$ ), and thus has sign  $\left( -1\right)  ^{n/2-1}$ . Since we know that it is an even permutation, we thus conclude that  $\left(  -1\right)  ^{n/2-1}=1$ . Therefore,  $n/2-1$  is even, so that  $n/2$  is odd. In other words,  $4\nmid n$ . This proves the `` $\Longrightarrow$ '' direction of the required implication. $\Longleftarrow:$  Assume that  $4\nmid n$ . Set  $m:=n/2$ . Then,  $2m=n$ , so that  $m$  is odd (since  $4\nmid n=2m$ ). We call an element of  $\mathbb{Z}/n$  \emph{even} if it is divisible by  $\overline{2}$  in  $\mathbb{Z}/n$  (that is, if it has the form  $\overline{u}$  for some even integer  $u$ ), and we call it \emph{odd} otherwise.

Let  $a$  be an integer coprime to  $n$ . Thus,  $a$  is odd (because if  $a$  was even, then  $a$  and  $n$  would both be even, so that  $a$  could not be coprime to  $n$ ). Hence,  $a+1$  is even. Therefore,  $\left(  a+1\right)  m$  is a multiple of  $2m=n$ . In other words,  $\left(  a+1\right)  m\equiv0\operatorname{mod}n$ .

Define a map  $\pi:\mathbb{Z}/n \to \mathbb{Z}/n$  by setting
\[
\pi\left(  x\right)  =
\begin{cases}
\overline{m}+ax, & \text{if }x\text{ is odd};
\overline{m}+x, & \text{if }x\text{ is even}
\end{cases}
\qquad \text{for each }x\in\mathbb{Z}/n.
\]


We claim the following:

\textit{Claim:} We have
\[
\pi\left(  \pi\left(  x\right)  \right)  =ax \qquad \text{for each }x\in\mathbb{Z}/n.
\]


\textit{Proof of the Claim:} Let  $x\in\mathbb{Z}/n$ . We must prove that  $\pi\left(  \pi\left(  x\right)  \right)  =ax$ . We are in one of the following two cases:

\textit{Case 1:} The element  $x$  is even.

\textit{Case 2:} The element  $x$  is odd.

Let us first consider Case 1. In this case,  $x$  is even. Hence, the definition of  $\pi$  yields  $\pi\left(  x\right)  =\overline{m}+x$ . Note that the sum of an odd and an even element of  $\mathbb{Z}/n$  is odd (since the same fact is true for integers). Thus, the element  $\overline{m}+x$  is odd (since  $m$  is odd but  $x$  is even). Hence, the definition of  $\pi$  yields  $\pi\left( \overline{m}+x\right)  =\overline{m}+a\left(  \overline{m}+x\right)  $ . Now,
\begin{align*}
\pi\left(  \underbrace{\pi\left(  x\right)  }_{=\overline{m}+x}\right)
&=\pi\left(  \overline{m}+x\right)  =\overline{m}+a\left(  \overline{m}+x\right)  =
\underbrace{\left(  a+1\right)  \overline{m}}_{\substack{=\overline{\left(  a+1\right)  m}=\overline{0}\text{(since }\left(  a+1\right)  m\equiv0\operatorname{mod}n\text{)}}}+\,ax
&  =\overline{0}+ax=ax.
\end{align*}
Thus, we have proved the Claim in Case 1.

A similar argument works in Case 2. Thus, the Claim is proved in all cases.

The Claim that we just proved shows that the map  $\pi\circ\pi$  is identical with the map
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{Z}/n  &   \to \mathbb{Z}/n,
x  &  \mapsto ax.
\end{align*}
But the latter map is a bijection (since  $a$  is coprime to  $n$ , and thus has a modular inverse in  $\mathbb{Z}/n$ ). Hence, the former map  $\pi\circ\pi$  is also a bijection. Therefore,  $\pi$  is a bijection, i.e., a permutation of  $\mathbb{Z}/n$ . Thus, we have found a permutation  $\pi$  of  $\mathbb{Z}/n$  such that  $\pi\left(  \pi\left(  x\right)  \right)  =ax$  for each  $x\in \mathbb{Z}/n$ . Hence, statement (B) holds. This proves the `` $\Longleftarrow$ '' direction of our equivalence.

Now, the equivalence (between statement (B) and  $4\nmid n$ ) is fully proved, and the problem is solved.</details>

According to the lemma, what you need is an $a$ whose Jacobi symbol is -1.

Is that easy to find? (for non-prime $n$ ).

First of all, the proof of Zolotarev's Lemma uses (at least IFAIK) primitive roots as well. You can either prove it directly or show that it's equivalent to the Gauss lemma for Jacobi symbols and then prove that, but both versions use the existence of primitive roots.

Second, the Jacobi symbol  $\left(\frac-n\right):(\mathbb Z/n)^\times\to\{\pm1\}$  for odd  $n$  is surjective iff  $n$  is not a square (this is trivial to see by the CRT), so this argument doesn't work for square  $n$ .

Personally I think the problem is nice, including the odd case. :thumbup:

$n=1$  obviously works. Suppose  $n\geq2$ . This is possible if and only if the permutation  $mk$  consists of some odd cycles and pairs of even cycles with the same size. For each  $d\mid n$ , the cycles formed from  $k$  such that  $\gcd(k,n)=\frac nd$  consist of  $\frac{\phi(d)}{\operatorname{ord}_d(m)}$  cycles of size  $\operatorname{ord}_d(m)$ . If  $m=-1$ , then  $\operatorname{ord}_d(m)=2$  for all  $d>2$ , so there are  $2$  cycles of size  $1$  and  $\frac{n-2}2$  cycles of size  $2$  if  $n$  is even and one cycle of size  $1$  and  $\frac{n-1}2$  cycles of size  $2$  if  $n$  is odd. Therefore,  $n\equiv2\pmod4$  or  $n\equiv1\pmod4$ . If  $n$  is odd, then pick some  $p^k\mid n$ . Let  $m$  be a primitive root modulo  $p^k$  and let  $m$  be  $1$  modulo every other prime power dividing  $n$ . Then,  $\operatorname{ord}_d(m)$  is equal to  $(p-1)p^{\nu_p(d)-1}$ . If  $d$  is not a power of  $p$ , then  $\frac{\phi(d)}{\operatorname{ord}_d(m)}$  is even. Otherwise, there will be exactly one cycle of size  $(p-1)p^{\nu_p(d)-1}$ , which means that the even cycles cannot be paired up.

Now, we will show that  $n\equiv2\pmod4$  satisfies the equations. If  $d$  is odd, we can pair the divisors of  $n$  into  $d$  and  $2d$ . Since  $\phi(d)=\phi(2d)$  and  $\operatorname{ord}_d(m)=\operatorname{ord}_{2d}(m)$ , we get that  $d$  and  $2d$  contribute the same number of cycles of each size, so all of the even cycles can be paired.

The motivation for the following solution is an attempt to compute  $\det(S)$  for small values of  $n$  by some Gaussian elimination. The entry  $S_{11}$  is almost never perturbed at the important early steps.

--------

The main observation is that  $S_{ij} = S_{ji} = s(i, j) = \mathbf{1}_{j \mid n} + \mathbf{1}_{j \mid n - i}$  for  $n \geq i > n/2$ , which holds since the equation  $ai + bj = n$  would force  $i \in \{0, 1\}$ . Here  $\mathbf{1}_{j \mid n}$  denotes the indicator function for the condition  $j \mid n$ .

Now assume that  $n \geq 5$ . For convenience, denote  $\mathcal{I} = \{n \in \mathbb{N} | n/2 < i < n - 1\} = \{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1, \ldots, n - 2\}$ .

Subtract the rows  $i \in \mathcal{I}$  with the row  $n - 1$ . We get a new matrix  $T$  with  $\det(T) = \det(S)$ , where  $T_{ij} = S_{ij} = s(i, j)$  for  $i \notin \mathcal{I}$ , and if  $i \in \mathcal{I}$  then
\[ T_{ij} = S_{ij} - S_{n - 1, j} = \mathbf{1}_{j \mid n - i} - \mathbf{1}_{j \mid 1} = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } j > 1 \text{ and } j \mid n - i,  0, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]
For example,


- row  $n - 2$  would be  $(0, 1, 0, 0, \ldots, 0)$ ,
- row  $n - 3$  would be  $(0, 0, 1, 0, 0, \ldots, 0)$ ,
- row  $n - 4$  would be  $(0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, \ldots, 0)$  if  $n \geq 9$ , etc.
[/list]
In particular, in the case  $i \in \mathcal{I}$ , we have  $T_{i, 1} = 0$ ,  $T_{i, n - i} = 1$ , and  $T_{i, j} = 0$  for all  $j > n - i$ . Now perform the row operations of form  $R_i \leftarrow R_i - T_{i, n - i'} R_{i'}$  across all  $n/2 < i < i' < n - 1$ , in a decreasing order (i.e.  $i' = n - 2, n - 3, \ldots$  and  $i = i' - 1, i' - 2, \ldots$ ) to get a new matrix  $U$ , but now with the rows  $i \in \mathcal{I}$  being the standard basis vector  $\mathbf{e}_{n - i}$ , where the entry  $n - i$  is  $1$  and all other entries are  $0$ . The matrix  $U$  satisfies  $\det(U) = \det(S)$ , and is a matrix with the following properties:
[list]
- $U_{ij} = S_{ij}$  if  $i \notin \mathcal{I}$ ,
- $U_{i, n - i} = 1$  if  $i \in \mathcal{I}$ ,
- $U_{i, j} = 0$  if  $i \in \mathcal{I}$  and  $j \neq n - i$ .


Now do the same thing with the columns  $j \in \mathcal{I}$ , except with column operations. Unfortunately, the entries at the block  $(U_{ij})$  for  $i, j \mathcal{I}$  has been perturbed, but all the other entries has not been changed. That is, for any  $j \in \mathcal{I}$ , we have
\[ U_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } i \in \mathcal{I},  S_{ji} = \mathbf{1}_{i | n} + \mathbf{1}_{i \mid n - j}, & \text{if } i \notin \mathcal{I} \end{cases} \]
Thus performing the column operations  $C_j \leftarrow C_j - C_{n - 1}$  gives a new matrix  $T'$  with  $\det(T') = \det(U) = \det(S)$  and
\[ T'_{ij} = \begin{cases} \mathbf{1}_{i + j = n}, & \text{if } i \in \mathcal{I},  S_{ij}, & \text{if } i, j \notin \mathcal{I},  0, & \text{if } i = 1 \text{ and } j \in \mathcal{I},  \mathbf{1}_{i \mid n - j}, & \text{if } i > 1, \; i \notin \mathcal{I}, \text{ and } j \in \mathcal{I}. \end{cases} \]
However, if  $i \in \mathcal{I}$  and  $j \in \mathcal{I}$ , then clearly  $\mathbf{1}_{i \mid n - j} = T'_{ij} = 0$  since  $n > i, j > n/2$ . So the condition  $i \notin \mathcal{I}$  in the last case above is superfluous. Doing the same process to obtain  $U$  from  $T$ , we get a matrix  $U'$  where  $\det(U) = \det(S)$ , and the entries have the following prescription:
\[ U'_{ij} = \begin{cases} \mathbf{1}_{i + j = n}, & \text{if } i \in \mathcal{I} \text{ or } j \in \mathcal{I},  S_{i, j}, & \text{if } i, j \notin \mathcal{I}. \end{cases} \]
For each  $j \in \mathcal{I}$ , Since the column  $j$  is the standard basis vector  $\mathbf{e}_{n - j}$ , we can eliminate all the other entries at row  $n - j$  without changing determinants. Similarly, we can eliminate all the entries at column  $n - j$  except the entry  $(j, n - j)$  without changing determinants. The resulting matrix, say  $V$ , satisfies  $\det(V) = \det(S)$ , with the following specification:
\[ V_{ij} = \begin{cases} \mathbf{1}_{i + j = n}, & \text{if } i \in \mathcal{I} \text{ or } j \in \mathcal{I} \text{ or } n - i \in \mathcal{I} \text{ or } n - j \in \mathcal{I},  S_{i, j}, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]
Notice that there are (at least)  $2 |\mathcal{I}|$  ones lying in the anti-diagonal of  $U'_{ij}$ , where all other entries in the same row or the same column as those ones are all zero. We now permute the rows so that they belong to the main diagonal; this needs  $|\mathcal{I}|$  swaps of form  $R_i \leftrightarrow R_{n - i}$  across all  $i \in \mathcal{I}$ . The new matrix  $W$  satisfies  $\det(W) = (-1)^{|\mathcal{I}|} \det(S)$ , where
\[ W_{ij} = \begin{cases} \mathbf{1}_{i = j}, & \text{if } i \in \mathcal{I} \text{ or } j \in \mathcal{I} \text{ or } n - i \in \mathcal{I} \text{ or } n - j \in \mathcal{I},  S_{i, j}, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]
Since  $|\mathcal{I}| = n - 2 - \lfloor n/2 \rfloor = \lceil n/2 \rceil - 2$ , it remains to show that  $\det(W) = - 2 \lceil n/2 \rceil$ . Now that the ones lie in the main diagonal, we can remove the rows and columns  $i$  with either  $i \in \mathcal{I}$  or  $n - i \in \mathcal{I}$ . For convenience, let
\[ \mathcal{J} = \{i \leq n : i \notin \mathcal{I}, n - i \notin \mathcal{I}\}. \]
Also, let  $A$  be the matrix obtained by removing the rows and columns  $i \in \mathcal{J}$  from  $W$ . Based on the above formula for the entries of  $W$ , we have  $\det(A) = \det(W)$ , and we can also obtain  $A$  by removing the rows and columns  $i \in \mathcal{J}$  from  $S$  instead of  $W$ . It now remains to show that  $\det(A) = -2 \lceil n/2 \rceil$ , and from now on we just use the indices in  $\mathcal{J}$ .

Note that for  $n = 3, 4$ , we can also follow this process, but it's identical as doing nothing.

--------

Now, for any  $1 \leq i \leq n$ , we have either  $i = n/2$  or  $i > n/2$  or  $n - i > n/2$ . So  $i, n - i \notin \mathcal{I}$  implies that  $i \in \{1, n/2, n - 1, n\}$ , where  $n/2$  appears only if  $n$  is even. Thus, we have  $\mathcal{J} = \{1, n - 1, n\}$  if  $n$  is odd and  $\mathcal{J} = \{1, n/2, n - 1, n\}$  if  $n$  is even. As a result, the matrix  $A$  has the following description:
\[ A = \begin{pmatrix} S_{1, 1} & S_{n - 1, 1} & S_{n, 1}  S_{1, n - 1} & S_{n - 1, n - 1} & S_{n, n - 1}  S_{1, n} & S_{n - 1, n} & S_{n, n} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} n + 1 & 2 & 2  2 & 0 & 1  2 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \text{if } 2 \nmid n \]
\[ A = \begin{pmatrix} S_{1, 1} & S_{n/2, 1} & S_{n - 1, 1} & S_{n, 1}  S_{1, n/2} & S_{n/2, n/2} & S_{n - 1, n/2} & S_{n, n/2}  S_{1, n - 1} & S_{n/2, n - 1} & S_{n - 1, n - 1} & S_{n, n - 1}  S_{1, n} & S_{n/2, n} & S_{n - 1, n} & S_{n, n} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} n + 1 & 3 & 2 & 2  3 & 3 & 1 & 2  2 & 1 & 0 & 1  2 & 2 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \text{if } 2 \mid n \]
Note that  $A$  is actually equal to  $S$  for  $n = 3, 4$ . Now we just do Gaussian elimination again to get  $\det(A) = -(n + 1)$  for the odd case and  $\det(A) = -n$  for the even case. Indeed,
\[ \begin{pmatrix} n + 1 & 2 & 2  2 & 0 & 1  2 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} n + 1 & 2 & 2  2 & 0 & 1  0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} n + 1 & 0 & 0  2 & 0 & 1  0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} n + 1 & 0 & 0  0 & 0 & 1  0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \]
\[ \begin{pmatrix} n + 1 & 3 & 2 & 2  3 & 3 & 1 & 2  2 & 1 & 0 & 1  2 & 2 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} n + 1 & 3 & 2 & 2  1 & 1 & 0 & 0  2 & 1 & 0 & 1  2 & 2 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} n + 1 & 3 & 2 & 2  1 & 1 & 0 & 0  2 & 1 & 0 & 1  0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} n & 0 & 0 & 0  1 & 1 & 0 & 0  2 & 1 & 0 & 1  0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} n & 0 & 0 & 0  0 & 1 & 0 & 0  0 & 1 & 0 & 1  0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \]

Thank you for your solution! I applied a similar idea during the contest but didn't finish it. The details in my solution are a bit different, though. For $k \not= 0$ , $\det M^{\sim k} = (-1)^{k - 1} \det U^{\sim k}$ where $U^{\sim k}$ is what we get by replacing the $k$ -th column of $M^{\sim 0}$ by all ones. By taking the combinatorial interpretation of determinants, we know that $\det U^{\sim k}$ is the sum of parities of all permutations $p$ on $[n]$ such that $p(i)$ divides $i$ for every $i$ except $i = k$ . Such permutations can only contain one cycle which is a decreasing sequence ending at $i$ . Therefore, we can write $M^{\sim k} (k \not= 0)$ explicitly as $(-1)^{k - 1} \det U^{\sim k} = \sum_{s_0 = k < s_1 < \dots < s_l \leq n, s_i | s_{i + 1}} (-1)^{l - 1} = (-1)^{k - 1}\sum_{1 \leq i \leq \frac{n}{k}} \mu(i)$ is the Mobius function (all the sequences that starts from $s_0$ and ends with $is_0$ have a total contribution $\mu(i)$ , which can be easily proved by induction). This directly leads to $M^{\sim k} = 1$ for $k > \frac{n}{2}$ . I came to this point during the contest and ran out of time (didn't even have time to write the proofs for the points above rigorously). In fact, after this, we can observe that for odd $n$ , $\sum_{i=0}^n M^{\sim k} M^{\sim (n - k)} = 2 (1 - \sum_{i=1}^{\frac{n - 1}{2}} \sum_{1 \leq j, ij \leq n} \mu(j)) = 2(1 - \sum_{i=1}^n (\sum_{j|i} \mu(j) - [i \geq \frac{n}{2}]))$ ; the same thing can be done for even $n$ . Also, I factorized $S$ into $MDM^T$ , where $D$ is the unit anti-diagonal matrix, which, for me, is a bit simpler to think about than showing $M$ and $N$ are equivalent. Note: I'm posting this for a friend of mine who doesn't have an AOPS account :)

Very nice problem! Here is a more algebraic solution inspired by the official solution. It bears some resemblance to the solutions above but the computations are a bit cleaner, with no need for Cauchy-Binet or any combinatorial arguments.

Throughout the solution, we will 1-index vector and matrix coordinates of total size  $n$  and 0-index vector and matrix coordinates of total size  $n+1$ . Note that  $S=AB^T$ , where  $A$  and  $B$  are  $n\times(n+1)$  matrices with entries  $a_{ij}=\mathbf1_{i\mid j}$  and  $b_{ij}=\mathbf1_{i\mid n-j}$ . The key observation is that  $\det(AB^T)$  is a linear function of the rows of  $A$  and  $B$  and vanishes whenever two of the rows of  $A$  are equal or two of the rows of  $B$  are equal. This implies that we may row reduce  $A$  and  $B$  to obtain sparser matrices  $A'$  and  $B'$  and instead compute  $\det(A'B'^T)$ .

To execute this, let  $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$  and  $w_1,\ldots,w_n\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$  be the rows of  $A$  and  $B$ . We then define  $v_i'=\sum_{ik\le n}\mu(k)v_{ik}$ , where  $\mu$  is the Mobius function. It is easy to see by the definition of the Mobius function that the entries of  $v_i'$  are given by  $(v_i')_0=\sum_{ik\le n}\mu(k)$ ,  $(v_i')_i=1$ , and  $(v_i')_j=0$  for  $j\ne0,i$ . Similarly, define  $w_i'=\sum_{ik\le n}\mu(k)w_{ik}$ , so the entries of  $w_i'$  are given by  $(w_i')_n=\sum_{ik\le n}\mu(k)$ ,  $(w_i')_{n-i}=1$ , and  $(w_i')_j=0$  for  $j\ne n,n-i$ . Let  $A'$  and  $B'$  be the matrices whose rows are given by  $v_1',\ldots,v_n'$  and  $w_1',\ldots,w_n'$ . Let  $c_i=\sum_{ik\le n}\mu(k)$ , so the entries  $s'(i,j)=v_i'\cdot w_j'$  of  $S'=A'B'^T$  are given by  $s'(i,n-i)=1$ ,  $s'(i,n)=s'(n,i)=c_i$  for  $i<n$ ,  $s'(n,n)=2$ , and  $s'(i,j)=0$  for all other  $i,j$ . Finally, let the rows of  $S'$  be  $u_1,\ldots,u_n$ , so  $u_n'=u_n-\sum_{i+j=n}c_iu_j$  has entries  $(u_n')_j=0$  for  $j<n$  and  $(u_n')_n=2-\sum_{i+j=n}c_ic_j$ . Thus,  $\det S=\det S'=(-1)^{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}\left(2-\sum_{i+j=n}c_ic_j\right)$ .

It remains to compute  $\sum_{i+j=n}c_ic_j$ . To do so, note that  $c_i=1$  for  $i>n/2$  and  $c_{n/2}=0$  if  $n$  is even, so  $\sum_{i+j=n}c_ic_j=2\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor}c_i=2\sum_{i=1}^n c_i-2\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor$ . On the other hand,  $\sum_{i=1}^nc_i=\sum_{ik\le n}\mu(i)=\sum_{m=1}^n\sum_{d\mid m}\mu(d)=1$ . Thus, the answer is  $(-1)^{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}2\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor$ .

I thought this problem was not particularly hard for B6. Below is a sketch of the solution I found during the contest. It just uses some elementary facts about matrices. 

Also, I think it is quite interesting that the answer is the same for  $2m-1$  and  $2m$ ; most solutions seem to differentiate between the odd and even case
---

Observe the following:



- When  $i + j > n$  and  $i, j < n$ ,  $S_{i,j} = 1$  when  $\min(i, j) \mid n$  and  $0$  otherwise.
- $S_{i, n} = 1$  if  $n/2 < i < n$ .
- $S_{1, i} = 2$  when  $n/2 < i < n$ .
[/list]

So, observe that if we subtract a multiple of row 1 from row  $i$  for  $2\leq i \leq n$  with  $i\mid n$ , and a multiple of column 1 from column  $i$  for  $2\leq i \leq n$ ,  $i\mid n$ , then we get a (symmetric) matrix  $S'$  with  $S'_{i, n} = 0$  for  $n/2 < i < n$ , and  $S'_{i, j} = 0$  for  $i+j > n$ ,  $i, j < n$ . At this point, we observe that \[
\det S = \det S' = \sum_{\pi \in S_n} \operatorname{sgn}(\pi) \prod S'_{i, \pi(i)}.
\]
Now, we consider which  $\pi$  can lead to a nonzero product. 
[list]
- $n$  odd: There is a bottom  $(n+1)/2$  by  $(n+1)/2$  with zeros except for  $S'_{n, n}$ . So, any nonzero permutation must have  $\pi(n) = n$ . Since the upper  $(n-1)$  by  $(n-1)$  matrix is triangular, we require  $\pi(i) = n-i$  for  $1\leq i \leq n-1$ .
- $n$  even: We have two cases: First, if  $\pi(n) = n$ , then again we require  $\pi(i) = n-i$  for  $1\leq i \leq n-1$ . Otherwise, we require  $\pi(\{1, 2, \ldots, n/2\}) = \{n/2 + 1, \ldots, n\}$  (and vice versa), so the only possibility for the upper right is  $\pi(1) = n-1, \ldots, \pi(n/2-1) = n/2 + 1$ ,  $\pi(n/2) = n$ . Likewise there is only one possibility for the lower left.

So, there are at most  $2$  values of  $\pi$  to evaluate. If we bookkeep the elements of  $S'$  appropriately, this is pretty doable.

I find it weird that the thread does not agree on the same answer as me, but my answer agrees with [https://kskedlaya.org/putnam-archive/2023s.pdf](this) (and it is correct for the case  $n=3$ , while ABCDE's don't seem to be correct for even that case)

We will assume  $n\ge 5$  for now. The main observation is that most of the entries don't matter. It's useful to really work out what happens when  $n$  is a large prime, but below solution will not use this assumption.

Observe that   $$  s(n-1, j) = \begin{cases}
2 & \text{ if } j = 1 
1 & \text{ if } j > 1 \text{ and } j\mid n 
0 & \text{ otherwise }
\end{cases} $$  More generally, if  $i+j>n, 2\le j<i<n$  then   $$  s(i, j) = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{ if } j > 1 \text{ and } j\mid n 
0 & \text{ otherwise }
\end{cases} $$  And for  $i>\frac n2$  we have  $s(i,1) = 2$ . 

The intuition is that the bottom rows look almost like a staircase, with row  $n-1$  as the base (when  $n$  is prime this is  $2,0,\cdots,0,1$ , but in other cases, it's more subtle, but it still serves as a base)

We will do some row and column removals such that the determinant of the altered matrix clearly help us recover the determinant of the original matrix, and reduce to a  $3\times 3$  matrix if  $n$  is odd and  $4\times 4$  matrix if  $n$  is even.

I claim that  $s(n-2,j) - s(n-1,j) = 1\{j=2\}$ . This is because  $s(n-2,1) = s(n-1,1) = 2$  since  $n\ge 5$ , and  $s(n-2,2) = 1 + 1\{2\mid n\}$  since  $(n-2)+2=n$  and  $0+2k=n$  iff  $n$  is even, while  $s(n-1,2) = 1\{2\mid n\}$  since  $(n-1)+2k=n$  has no solutions and  $0+2k=n$  iff  $n$  even. For  $j\ge 3$ , note that this follows from the above characterization. 

Thus we can do  $R_{n-2} \leftarrow R_{n-2}-R_{n-1}$ , remove column 2 and row  $n-2$ . Analogously, we can remove row 2 and column  $n-2$ . After these two steps, we get a matrix with rows and columns labelled  $[n] \setminus \{2,n-2\}$ , and the determinant of this matrix is  $-1$  times the determinant of the original matrix, since the unique  $1$ 's in  $(2,n-2)$  and  $(n-2,2)$  form a 2-cycle, which is an odd permutation. (Note the symmetrization trick is kinda important when we are dealing with symmetric matrices)

Now, if  $n-3 > \frac n2$ , then we can analogously compare row  $n-3$  with row  $n-1$  without looking at column 2. We can see that  $s(n-3,j) - s(n-1,j) = 1\{j=3\}$  when  $j\ge 3$ . Thus we remove rows  $3,n-3$  and columns  $3,n-3$ . 

We can do this and remove rows and columns  $2,\cdots, \lfloor \frac{n-1}{2}\rfloor, n-\lfloor \frac{n-1}{2}\rfloor, \cdots, n-2$ . Note the entries in the other rows or columns DO NOT CHANGE. We removed  $\lfloor \frac{n-3}{2}\rfloor$  pairs of rows and columns, so the determinant of this 3x3 or 4x4 matrix is  $(-1)^{\lfloor \frac{n-3}{2}\rfloor}$  times the determinant of the original matrix. 

If  $n$  is odd, this matrix (I will label the rows or column with  $1,n-1,n$ ) is   $$  \begin{bmatrix}
n+1 & 2 & 2 
2 & 0 & 1 
2 & 1 & 2
\end{bmatrix} $$  The determinant of this matrix is  $-(n+1)$ . Thus when  $n\ge 3$  is odd, the answer is  $(-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}(n+1)$ If  $n$  is even, this matrix (I will label the rows or column with  $1,\frac n2, n-1,n$ ) is   $$  \begin{bmatrix}
n+1 & 3 & 2 & 2 
3 & 3 & 1 & 2 
2 & 1 & 0 & 1 
2 & 2 & 1 & 2
\end{bmatrix} $$  This matrix has determinant  $-n$ . Hence the determinant of this matrix is  $(-1)^{\frac{n}{2}+1}n$ .

stem_md: A solid in Euclidean  $3$ -space extends from  $z = \frac{-h}{2}$  to  $z = \frac{+h}{2}$  and the area of the section  $z = k$  is a polynomial in  $k$  of degree at most  $3$ . Show that the volume of the solid is  $\frac{h(B + 4M + T)}{6},$  where  $B$  is the area of the bottom  $(z = \frac{-h}{2})$ ,  $M$  is the area of the middle section  $(z = 0),$  and  $T$  is the area of the top  $(z = \frac{h}{2})$ . Derive the formulae for the volumes of a cone and a sphere.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Let the area of the solid at  $z=k$  is  $P(k)=ak^3+bk^2+ck+d$ , then the volume of the solid is given by  $\int_{-\frac{h}{2}}^{\frac{h}{2}}P(k) dk = \int_{-\frac{h}{2}}^{\frac{h}{2}}(ak^3+bk^2+ck+d) dk=\int_{-\frac{h}{2}}^{\frac{h}{2}}(bk^2+d) dk=\frac{2b}{3}\cdot \left(\frac{h}{2}\right)^3+2d\cdot \frac{h}{2}=\frac{h}{6}\cdot \left(\frac{bh^2}{2}+6d\right)$ .

So we have to prove that  $\frac{bh^2}{2}+6d=B+4M+T$ . Here we have: $B=P\left(-\frac{h}{2}\right)=a\left(-\frac{h}{2}\right)^3+b\left(-\frac{h}{2}\right)^2+c\left(-\frac{h}{2}\right)+d$  $M=P(0)=d$  $T=P\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)=a\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)^3+b\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)^2+c\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)+d$ And then  $B+4M+T=\frac{bh^2}{2}+6d$ Q.E.D.</details>

Then the volume of the solid is  $$ \int_{-h/2}^{h/2} (a_0 + a_1k + a_2k^2 + a_3k^3) \, dk = \int_{-h/2}^{h/2} (a_0 + a_2k^2) \, dk = a_0h + \frac{a_2}{12}h^3; $$  note that the odd terms cancel out. stem_md: A solid has a cylindrical middle with a conical cap at each end. The height of each cap equals the length of the middle. For a given surface area, what shape maximizes the volume?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Let  $r$  be the base radius of cylinder, so it radius of base of the conics,  $h$  is the height of cylinder. Let  $S$  be the area of the given solid,  then: $S=2\cdot \pi r\sqrt{r^2+h^2}+2\pi rh$ .
The volume  $V$  of the solid is equal to  $\frac{2h \pi r^2}{3}+\pi r^2h$ . So we have to find the maximum of the  $V$  by the given  $S$ . $(S-2\pi hr)^2=4\pi^2 r^2 (r^2+h^2)$  $S^2-4S\pi hr+4\pi^2h^2r^2=4\pi^2r^4+4\pi^2r^2h^2$  $S^2-4S\pi hr=4\pi^2r^4$  $h=\frac{S^2-4\pi^2r^4}{4S\pi r}$  $V=\frac{2\pi r^2}{3}\cdot \frac{S^2-4\pi^2r^4}{4S\pi r} + \pi r^2\cdot \frac{S^2-4\pi^2r^4}{4S\pi r}=\frac{2S^2\pi r^2-8\pi^3r^6+3\pi r^2S^2-12\pi^3r^6}{12S\pi r}=\frac{5S^2 r-20\pi^2r^5}{12S}$ .
And so  $V=V(r)$ , then  $V'=\frac{5S}{12}-\frac{25\pi^2r^4}{3S}=0$  gives us  $r^4=\frac{S^2}{20\pi^2}$ , then  $r=\sqrt[4]{\frac{S^2}{20\pi^2}}=r_0$  and therefore when  $r>r_0 => V'<0$  and when  $r<r_0$  we have  $V'>0$ , then  $r=r_0$  is the point of maximum.
Then $h=\frac{S}{4\pi}\cdot \frac{\sqrt[4]{20\pi^2}}{\sqrt[4]{S^2}}-\frac{\pi}{S}\cdot \left(\frac{S^2}{20\pi^2}\right)^3$</details>

stem_md: A particle moves in the Euclidean plane. At time  $t$  (taking all real values) its coordinates are  $x = t^3 - t$  and  $y = t^4 + t.$  Show that its velocity has a maximum at  $t = 0,$  and that its path has an inflection at  $t = 0.$
solution_md: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press.**First Solution.** If the velocity vector at time $t$ is of length $v$ and has direction $\theta,$ then $\dot x = v \cos \theta, \dot y = v \sin \theta,$ and $\ddot x = \dot v \cos \theta - v \dot \theta \sin \theta,$ $\ddot y = \dot v \sin \theta + v \dot \theta \cos \theta.$ Thus $\dot x \ddot y - \dot y \ddot x = v^2 \dot \theta$ and $v^2 = {\dot x}^2 + {\dot y}^2.$ From the given parametric data, \begin{align*} v^2 \dot \theta &= (3t^2- 1) 12t^2 - (4t^3 + 1)6t = 6t(2t^3- 2t - 1) v^2 &= 16t^6 + 9t^4 + 8t^3 - 6t^2 + 2.\end{align*} From the $v^2\dot\theta$ relation, $\dot\theta$ changes sign as $t$ passes through $0.$ To rule out the possibility of a cusp point, one notes that $v^2 \neq 0$ at $t =0.$ Hence the curve has an inflection point at $t=0.$ Also \begin{align*} \frac{\mathrm d(v^2)}{\mathrm dt} &= 96t^5 + 36t^4 + 24t^2 - 12t \frac{\mathrm d(v^2)}{\mathrm dt} \bigg ]_{t=0} &= 0 \end{align*} and \[\frac{\mathrm d^2 (v^2)}{\mathrm dt^2} \bigg ]_{t=0} = -12.\] So $v^2$ has a (local) maximum at $t = 0.$ Hence the speed $v$ also has a local maximum.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/MAA AMC/Putnam/Putnam 1938/2652904.json

candidates: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press.**Second Solution.** Since $\mathrm dx / \mathrm dt$ does not vanish for $t=0,$ we can solve for $t$ in terms of $x$ near $t = 0$ and write $y$ as a function of $x.$ Then we have \[\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} = \frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt} \bigg / \frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt} = \frac{4t^3 + 1}{3t^2 - 1} = -1 - 3t^2 - \cdots.\] Therefore, $\mathrm dy/\mathrm dx$ has a (local) maximum at $t =0,$ so the curve has an inflection poin ta t $t = 0.$ The magnitude $v$ of the velocity is given by \[v^2 = \left(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt} \right)^2 + \left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}\right)^2 = (3t^2 - 1)^2+ (4t^3 + 1)^2 = 2 - 6t^2 + \cdots.\] Hence $v$ has a (local) maximum at $t = 0.$

stem_md: A swimmer is standing at a corner of a square swimming pool. She swims at a fixed speed and runs at a fixed speed (possibly different). No time is taken entering or leaving the pool. What path should she follow to reach the opposite corner of the pool in the shortest possible time?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Direct solution</summary>Let  $s$  and  $r$  be real numbers, where  $s$  is understood as the swimming speed and  $r$  the running speed. Let  $P$  denote the closed unit square (and its interior) in  $\mathbb{R}^2$  with vertices  $A(0,0),B(1,0),C(1,1),D(0,1)$ , understood as the space of the pool amongst land in all directions. Let  $X=(1/2,1/2)$ .

Consider all paths from  $A$  to  $C$ . For any given path  $\gamma$ , we may partition the path into a set of subpaths delineated by each intersection with  $\partial P$ . Let  $\textrm{In}(\gamma)$  be the set of subpaths inside  $P$ , and  $\textrm{Out}(\gamma)$  the set of paths on  $\partial P$  or outside  $P$ . Let  $L(\gamma$ ) denote the arc length of a path. Define a function  $T$  from all paths to real numbers such that   $$ T(\gamma)=\frac1s\sum_{x\in\textrm{In}(\gamma)}L(x)+\frac1r\sum_{x\in\textrm{Out}(\gamma)}L(x), $$   returning what is understood as the time elapsed traveling the path. Given  $s$  and  $r$ , we seek a path that minimizes  $T$ .
	
We can start with a few simplifications. First, we may assume the path lies strictly in  $P$ , as any path that ventures outside  $P$  can trivially be shortened by hugging  $\partial P$ . Second, notice the path must intersect  $\overline{BD}$  by continuity. Clearly, there exists a minimal path no matter the values of  $a$  and  $b$ . Let  $E$  be an intersection of a minimal path with  $\overline{BD}$ . This divides that minimal path into two subpaths. If either subpath were shorter than the other, it could be reflected over line  $BD$  and replace the other subpath, creating an overall shorter path, contradicting the minimality of the path. Consequently, the subpaths must be the same length. Thus, we may replace reflect the subpath from  $A$  to  $E$  over  $BD$  and replace the subpath from  $E$  to  $C$  with the result without changing the length of the overall path. So we may assume minimal paths are symmetric with respect to  $BD$  and focus only on paths from  $A$  to  $\overline{BD}$ . Third, these paths may or may not intersect  $\overline{AX}$  (at points other than  $A$  and  $X$ ). If they do, we may reflect the resultant subpaths above  $AC$  over  $AC$  to get a new path of the same length but contained entirely in the triangle  $ABX$ . So we may assume minimal paths are restricted to this triangle and find the minimal path in  $ABX$  from  $A$  to  $\overline{BX}$ .
	
Now we are at the heart of the problem. Any path will be a finite sequence of subpaths along the boundary (running) and subpaths along the interior (swimming). Denote subpaths of the former type with an  $R$  and the latter type with an  $S$ . So any path is a finite string of  $R$ 's and  $S$ 's, such as  $SRSRS$ . Observe that if  $r>s$ , the rule  $SR\to R$  always saves time. Given this rule along with  $RR\to R$  and  $SS\to S$ , we can assume minimal paths where  $r>s$  are of the form  $RS$ . When  $s\geq r$ , the path should clearly just be  $\overline{AX}$ . Note also that when  $r$  is large enough in proportion to  $s$ , we technically just do  $R$ . If we let an  $R$  and an  $S$  both possibly be just points, then  $RS$  actually covers all choices of  $r$  and  $s$ . By the Pythagorean theorem, in a minimal path, the  $S$  subpath should be normal to line  $BX$ . The path is now a fixed shape. Let  $x$  be the distance leftover to  $B$  when we leave the boundary and begin  $S$ . This means  $R$  is  $1-x$  in length, and, using a  $45^{\circ}$ - $45^{\circ}$ - $90^{\circ}$  right triangle,  $S$  is  $x/\sqrt2$ . This means for a minimal path  $\gamma'$ , we have   $$ T(\gamma')=\frac1s\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt2}\right)+\frac1r(1-x)=\frac1r+\left(\frac1{s\sqrt2}-\frac1r\right)x. $$   Now, it easy to see that if  $r>\sqrt{2}s$ , we get a minimal path for  $x=0$ , which corresponds to just running around the boundary, and otherwise, we get a minimal path for  $x=1$ , which is just swimming the diagonal.</details>
<details><summary>Indirect solution</summary>Let  $P$  denote the closed square (and its interior) in  $\mathbb{R}^2$  with vertices  $A(0,0),B(1/2,1/2),C(0,1),D(-1/2,-1/2)$ , understood as the space of the pool amongst land in all directions. We seek a minimal path from  $A$  to  $C$ .

Any path that exits  $P$  returns at some point--you can trivially shorten such paths by replacing the excursion out of  $P$  with lines that hug  $\partial P$ . So we may assume the minimal path stays in  $P$ . Say the ratio of her run speed to her swim speed is less than  $\sqrt2$ . Consider the diagonal path  $\overline{AC}$ . Now, take any other path and draw lines parallel to the  $x$ -axis passing through all its entry and exit points to and from  $\partial P$  (places where she runs along the edge). These lines separate the diagonal path and our other path into subpaths that lie strictly between consecutive parallels. (and in case the other path doubles back on itself, possibly multiple subpaths). Compare the time elapsed in each pair of corresponding subpaths. The diagonal is always faster. Aside from this, the other path may also spend some time exactly coincident with a parallel, which just makes things worse for the other path. So the diagonal is clearly fastest. Now, say the ratio of her run speed to her swim speed is greater than  $\sqrt2$ . Consider either path going along the boundary. Now do the same analysis as before. Swimming subpaths normal to the parallels are fastest, but even those are slower than the subpaths along the boundary at the given run speed. All subpaths of just swimming between parallels are longer than these normals. Further, the remaining subpaths, those that are just running, take the same amount of time. And again, the other path could only do worse beyond this, possibly doubling back on itself or running coincident to the parallels. So the boundary is clearly best. If the ratio is exactly  $\sqrt{2}$ , she can do whatever combination of swimming parallel to the diagonal and running along the boundary she wants, but if she wanted to be simple, she could just stick with either the diagonal or the boundary.</details>

Let  $B$  be the  $4 \times 4$  matrix  $(A_{ij})$  and let  $D$  be det  $B.$  Prove  $D = d^3$ . $(2)$    Let  $P(x)$  be the quadratic  $Ax^2 + Bx + C.$  Suppose that  $P(x) = x$  has unequal real roots. Show that the roots are also roots of  $P(P(x)) = x.$  Find a quadratic equation for the other two roots of this equation. Hence solve  $(y^2 - 3y + 2)2 - 3(y^2 - 3y + 2) + 2 - y = 0.$
solution_md: (2) Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. Since $a$ is a root of $P(y) - y = 0,$ we have $P(a) = a.$ Then $P(P(a)) = P(a) = a,$ so $a$ is a root of $P(P(y)) - y = 0.$ Similarly, $b$ is a root of this biquadratic. Let $Q(y) = P(P(y)) - y.$ To find the other zeros of $Q,$ note that $P(y) - y = Ay^2 + (B - 1)y + C = A(y - a)(y - b),$ whence $A(a + b) = 1 - B.$ Then \begin{align*} Q(y) &= P(P(y)) - P(y) + P(y) - y &= A \{ P(y) - a\} \{P(y) - b\} + A(y - a)(y - b) &= A \{A (y - a)(y - b) + y - a \} \{A (y - a)(y - b) + y - b \} + A(y- a)(y - b) &= A(y - a)(y - b) R(y),\end{align*} where \begin{align*} R(y) &= \{ A(y - b) + 1 \}\{A(y - a)+ 1\} + 1 &= AP(y) + Ay - A(a + b) + 2 &= A^2 y^2 + A(B + 1)y + AC + B + 1. \end{align*} The roots $c$ and $d$ are the zeros of $R,$ so the required quadratic equation for $c$ and $d$ is \[A^2 y^2 + A(B+ 1)y + AC+ B + 1 = 0.\] In the special case gievn, $A= 1, B = -3, C = 2,$ and $R(y) = y^2 - 2y.$ The zeros of $P(y) - y$ are $2 \pm \sqrt 2,$ so the zeros of $Q$ are $2 \pm \sqrt2, 0,$ and $2.$

stem_md: Find all solutions of the differential equation  $zz" - 2z'z' = 0$  which pass through the point  $x=1, z=1.$
solution_md: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press.**First Solution.** $1/y^3$ is an integrating factor since \[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx} \left( \frac{y'}{y^2} \right) = \frac{y y'' - 2(y')^2}{y^3} = 0.\] Therefore $y'/y^2 = C$ and $-1/y = Cx + D$ for appropriate constants $C$ and $D.$ In order that the solution pass through $(1, 1),$ we require that $C + D = -1.$ Hence \[\tag{1} y = \frac 1{1 + C(1 - x)}.\] Conversely, any function of this form satisfies the equation and the initial conditions. If $C =0,$ this is a constant function and its domain may be taken as $(-\infty, +\infty).$ If $C \neq 0,$ the right member of $(1)$ becomes infinite for $x = (1 + C)/C,$ so the domain of $(1)$ must be restricted to \[\left(- \infty, \frac {1 + C}C \right) \text{ if } C > 0; \qquad \left( \frac {1 + C}C, \infty \right) \text{ if } C < 0.\]

stem_md: The parabola  $P$  has focus a distance  $m$  from the directrix. The chord  $AB$  is normal to  $P$  at  $A.$  What is the minimum length for  $AB?$
solution_md: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. Any point on the parabola has coordinates of the form $(2mt^2, 2mt).$ Say $A = (2mt^2, 2mt)$ and $B = (2ms^2, 2ms).$ The slope of $AB$ is $\dfrac 1{s + t}$ and the slope of the tangent at $A$ is $\dfrac 1{2t}.$ Hence $s + t = - \dfrac 1{2t}.$ The length $L$ of $AB$ is given by \[L^2 = 4m^2 [(s^2 - t^2)^2 + (s - t)^2] = 4m^2 (s - t)^2 [(s + t)^2 + 1].\] Substituting $s = -t - \dfrac 1{2t}$ we have \[\tag{1} L^2 = 4m^2 \left( \frac{4t^2 + 1}{2t} \right)^2 \frac{1 + 4t^2}{4t^2} = \frac {m^2}{4} \, \frac{(4t^2 + 1)^3}{t^4}.\] We seek the value of $t$ which minimizes $L,$ so we may just as well choose $t$ to minimize \[ \frac{4t^2 + 1}{t^{4/3}} = 4t^{2/3} + t^{-4/3}.\] Setting the derivative equal to zero, we find two critical points, $t = \pm \dfrac {\sqrt 2}2.$ Since $L \to \infty$ as $t \to 0, \pm \infty,$ these two critical values both give minima. Either of the two shortest chords is of length $3 \sqrt 3 |m|,$ from $(1).$

stem_md: Find the locus of the foot of the perpendicular from the center of a rectangular hyperbola to a tangent. Obtain its equation in polar coordinates and sketch it.
solution_md: Without loss of generality, let the rectangular hyperbola be   $$ xy=1\implies (x,y)=\left(t,\frac{1}{t}\right),\,t\in\mathbb{R}. $$   Its center is at  $(0,0).$  Now   $$ xy=1\implies y+x\frac{dy}{dx}=0\implies\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{y}{x}. $$   So equation of tangent at point  $\left(t,\frac{1}{t}\right)$  is given by   $$ y-\frac{1}{t}=-\frac{\frac{1}{t}}{t}(x-t)\implies t^2y-t=t-x\implies x+t^2y-2t=0. $$   Let the foot of perpendicular to the above straight line from center  $(0,0)$  be  $(h,k).$  Then   $$ k=t^2h\implies h+t^4h-2t=0\implies h=\frac{2t}{1+t^4}\implies k=\frac{2t^3}{1+t^4} $$     $$ \implies \frac{k}{h}=t^2\quad\&\quad hk=\frac{4t^4}{(1+t^4)^2}=\frac{4\left(\frac{k}{h}\right)^2}{\left(1+\left(\frac{k}{h}\right)^2\right)^2}=\frac{4h^2k^2}{(h^2+k^2)^2} $$     $$ \implies (h^2+k^2)^2=4hk $$   since  $hk\ne 0.$  For polar coordinates, putting  $h=r\cos\theta$  and  $k=r\sin\theta$  gives   $$ r^4=4r^2\cos\theta\sin\theta\implies r^2=2\sin(2\theta). $$

stem_md: What is the shortest distance between the plane  $Ax + By + Cz + 1 = 0$  and the ellipsoid  $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} + \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1.$  You may find it convenient to use the notation  $h = (A^2 + B^2 + C^2)^{\frac{-1}{2}}, m = (a^2A^2 + b^2B^2 + c^2C^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}.$  What is the algebraic condition for the plane not to intersect the ellipsoid?
solution_md: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. If the given plane intersects the ellipsoid, then the minimum distance is zero. If the plane fails to intersect the ellipsoid, then the shortest distance is the distance between the given plane and the nearer of the two tangent planes to the ellipsoid that are parallel to the given plane. The tangent plane to the ellipsoid at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is \[\frac{x_0 x}{a^2 } + \frac{y_0 y}{b^2} + \frac{z_0 z}{c^2} = 1.\] If this plane is parallel to $Ax + By + Cz + 1 = 0,$ then \[ \frac{x_0}{a^2} = kA, \quad \frac{y_0}{b^2} = kB, \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{z_0}{c^2} = kC,\] where $k$ is a constant. Since \[1 = \frac{{x_0}^2}{a^2} + {{y_0}^2}{b^2} + \frac{{z_0}^2}{c^2} = k^2 [a^2 A^2 + b^2 B^2 + c^2 C^2],\] we get $|k| = \dfrac 1m.$ The distance from the origin to the given plane is \[\frac 1{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}} = h.\] Since the parallel tangent plane can be written in the form \[ k(Ax + By + Cz) = 1,\] the distance from the origin to either parallel tangent plane is \[ \frac 1{|k| \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}} = hm.\] Hence if $m < 1,$ the given plane lies farther from the origin than the tangent planes, and it does not cut the ellipsoid. The distance from the ellipsoid to the given plane in this case is $h(1- m).$ But if $m \ge 1,$ the given plane either lies between the tangent planes or coincides with one of them, so it cuts the ellipsoid and the distance is zero.

stem_md: Let  $C$  be the curve  $y^2 = x^3$  (where  $x$  takes all non-negative real values). Let  $O$  be the origin, and  $A$  be the point where the gradient is  $1.$  Find the length of the curve from  $O$  to  $A.$
solution_md:
Observe that $$ y^2=x^3\implies 2y\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2\implies\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3x^2}{2y}. $$ So the point $A$ with gradient $1$ should lie on the first quadrant. The parametric for of the curve in the first quadrant is $(x,y)=(t^2,t^3),\,t\ge 0.$ So, the gradient at point $(t^2,t^3)$ is $$ \frac{3t^4}{2t^3}=\frac{3t}{2}. $$ Hence, the parameter at point $A$ is $t=\frac{2}{3}.$ In the first quadrant, the curve is equivalent to $$ y=x^{3/2}\implies \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3\sqrt{x}}{2}. $$ So length of the curve from $O$ to $A$ is $$ \ell=\int_0^{2/3}\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}dx=\int_0^{2/3}\sqrt{1+\frac{9x}{4}}dx $$ $$ =\frac{4}{9}\int_0^{2/3}\sqrt{1+\frac{9x}{4}}d\left(1+\frac{9x}{4}\right)=\frac{8}{27}\left[\left(1+\frac{9x}{4}\right)^{3/2}\right]_0^{2/3}=\frac{10\sqrt{10}-8}{27}. $$

stem_md: Let  $C$  be the curve  $y = x^3$  (where  $x$  takes all real values). The tangent at  $A$  meets the curve again at  $B.$  Prove that the gradient at  $B$  is  $4$  times the gradient at  $A.$
solution_md: Reproduced from Gleason-Greenwood-Kelly, MAA press. Let $P$ have coordinates $(x_0,y_0);$ then the slope at $P$ is $3{x_0}^2.$ The equation of the tangent at $P$ is $y = 3{x_0}^2 (x - x_0) + {x_0}^3.$ The points of intersection of the tangent and the original curve are determined by the relation \[x^3 = 3{x_0}^2 (x - x_0) + {x_0}^3,\] which is equivalent to \[(x - x_0)^2 (x + 2x_0) = 0.\] Hence the second point of intersection is $(-2x_0, -8{x_0}^3).$ The slope at this point is $12{x_0}^2,$ which is four times the slope at $P,$ as was to be proved. If $x_0 = 0,$ the tangent does not really meet the curve again. However, since the tangent in this case has a triple point of intersection with the curve, instead of the usual double point of intersection, it is reasonable to say that it meets the curve "again" at $(0,0).$

stem_md: The roots of  $x^3 + a x^2 + b x + c = 0$  are  $\alpha, \beta$  and  $\gamma.$  Find the cubic whose roots are  $\alpha^3, \beta^3, \gamma^3.$
solution_md:
By vieta's we have  $$ \alpha + \beta + \gamma = -a $$    $$ \alpha \beta + \beta \gamma + \gamma \alpha = b $$    $$ \alpha \beta \gamma = -c $$  Let our desired cubic be  $x^3 - dx^2 + ex - f$ , where  $d=\sum _{cyc} \alpha ^3$ ,  $e = \sum _{cyc} \alpha ^3 \beta ^3$ , and  $f = \alpha ^3 \beta ^3 \gamma ^3$ . Clearly  $f = -c^3$ .

For  $d$  consider the following  $$ (\alpha + \beta + \gamma)^2 = \alpha ^2 + \beta ^2 + \gamma ^2 + 2(\alpha \beta + \beta \gamma + \gamma \alpha) $$     $$ \Rightarrow \alpha ^2 + \beta ^2 + \gamma ^2 = a^2 - 2b $$    $$ \Rightarrow (\alpha ^2 + \beta ^2 + \gamma ^2)(\alpha + \beta + \gamma) = (a^2 - 2b)(-a) $$    $$ \Rightarrow \alpha ^3 + \beta ^3 + \gamma ^3 + \alpha ^2 \beta + \alpha ^2 \gamma + \beta ^2 \alpha + \beta ^2 \gamma + \gamma ^2 \alpha + \gamma ^2 \beta = -a^3 + 2ab \textbf{ (I)} $$    $$ (\alpha + \beta + \gamma)^3 = \alpha ^3 + \beta ^3 + \gamma ^3 + 6 \alpha \beta \gamma + 3(\alpha ^2 \beta + \alpha ^2 \gamma + \beta ^2 \alpha + \beta ^2 \gamma + \gamma ^2 \alpha + \gamma ^2 \beta ) $$    $$ \Rightarrow -a^3 + 6c = \alpha ^3 + \beta ^3 + \gamma ^3 + 3(\alpha ^2 \beta + \alpha ^2 \gamma + \beta ^2 \alpha + \beta ^2 \gamma + \gamma ^2 \alpha + \gamma ^2 \beta ) \textbf{ (II)} $$    $$ 3\textbf{(I) } - \textbf{ (II)} = 2(\alpha ^3 + \beta ^3 + \gamma ^3) = 3(-a^3 + 2ab) - (-a^3 + 6c) $$    $$ \Rightarrow \alpha ^3 + \beta ^3 + \gamma ^3 = -a^3 + 3ab - 3c = d $$  Similarly for  $e$  we have  $$ (\alpha \beta + \beta \gamma + \gamma \alpha)^2 = \alpha ^2 \beta ^2 + \beta ^2 \gamma ^2 + \gamma ^2 \alpha ^2 + 2(\alpha ^2 \beta \gamma + \alpha \beta ^2\gamma + \alpha \beta \gamma ^2) $$    $$ \Rightarrow \alpha ^2 \beta ^2 + \beta ^2 \gamma ^2 + \gamma ^2 \alpha ^2 = b^2 -2ac $$    $$ \Rightarrow (\alpha ^2 \beta ^2 + \beta ^2 \gamma ^2 + \gamma ^2 \alpha ^2 )(\alpha \beta + \beta \gamma + \gamma \alpha) = b^3 - 2abc $$    $$ \Rightarrow \alpha ^3 \beta ^3 + \beta ^3 \gamma ^3 + \gamma ^3 \alpha ^3 + \alpha \beta \gamma(\alpha ^2 \beta + \alpha ^2 \gamma + \beta ^2 \alpha + \beta ^2 \gamma + \gamma ^2 \alpha + \gamma ^2 \beta) = b^3 - 2abc $$  From  $\textbf{(I)}$  we have  $$ \alpha ^2 \beta + \alpha ^2 \gamma + \beta ^2 \alpha + \beta ^2 \gamma + \gamma ^2 \alpha + \gamma ^2 \beta = -a^3 + 2ab - (\alpha ^3 + \beta ^3 + \gamma ^3) = 3c - ab $$  Thus, we have  $$ \alpha ^3 \beta ^3 + \beta ^3 \gamma ^3 + \gamma ^3 \alpha ^3 + \alpha \beta \gamma(\alpha ^2 \beta + \alpha ^2 \gamma + \beta ^2 \alpha + \beta ^2 \gamma + \gamma ^2 \alpha + \gamma ^2 \beta) = b^3 - 2abc $$    $$ \Rightarrow \alpha ^3 \beta ^3 + \beta ^3 \gamma ^3 + \gamma ^3 \alpha ^3 -c(3c-ab) = b^3 - 2abc $$    $$ \Rightarrow \alpha ^3 \beta ^3 + \beta ^3 \gamma ^3 + \gamma ^3 \alpha ^3 = b^3 + 3c^2 - 3abc = e $$  Finally, our desired polynomial is  $$ x^3 - dx^2 + ex - f $$    $$ = \boxed{x^3 + (a^3 - 3ab + 3c)x^2 + (b^3 + 3c^2 - 3abc)x + c^3} $$

The roots of $x^3 + a x^2 + b x + c = 0$ are $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma.$ Find the cubic whose roots are $\alpha^3, \beta^3, \gamma^3.$
Just take the characteristic polynomial of the cube of the companion matrix of $x^3+ax^2+bx+c$ .
Put y=  $x^3$  and eliminate x between the two equations. The eliminant is the required equation.

stem_md: Do either  $(1)$  or  $(2)$ : $(1)$    Let  $C_a$  be the curve  $(y - a^2)^2 = x^2(a^2 - x^2).$  Find the curve which touches all  $C_a$  for  $a > 0.$  Sketch the solution and at least two of the  $C_a.$  $(2)$    Given that  $(1 - hx)^{-1}(1 - kx)^{-1} = \sum_{i\geq0}a_i x^i,$  prove that  $(1 + hkx)(1 - hkx)^{-1}(1 - h^2x)^{-1}(1 - k^2x)^{-1} = \sum_{i\geq0}  a_i^2 x^i.$
solution_md:
Given  $(y-a^{2})^{2} = x^{2}(a^{2} - x^{2})$ .

We calculate the derivative w.r.t.  $a\ :\ 2(y-a^{2})(-2a)=x^{2}(2a)$ and we solve  $a^{2}=y+\frac{x^{2}}{2}$ .

In the given equation, we find  $y=\frac{3}{4}x^{2}$ .

solution_md:
Given the curve  $\frac{y}{c} = \cosh (\frac{x}{c})$  or  $y=\frac{c}{2}(e^{\frac{x}{c}}+e^{-\frac{x}{c}})$ .

On this curve  $Q(0,c)$  and  $P(a,b)$ , so  $b=\frac{c}{2}(e^{\frac{a}{c}}+e^{-\frac{a}{c}})$ . $y'=\frac{1}{2}(e^{\frac{x}{c}}-e^{-\frac{x}{c}})$ .
Equation of the line, through  $Q$  and  $//$  normal in  $P\ :\ y-c=\frac{2}{e^{\frac{a}{c}}-e^{-\frac{a}{c}}} \cdot x$ .

Point  $R(\frac{c}{2}(e^{\frac{a}{c}}-e^{-\frac{a}{c}}),0)$ .
Distance  $QR\ =\ \sqrt{\frac{c^{2}}{4}(e^{\frac{a}{c}}-e^{-\frac{a}{c}})^{2}+c^{2}}=\frac{c}{2}(e^{\frac{a}{c}}+e^{-\frac{a}{c}})=b$ .

stem_md: Given    $a_n = (n^2 + 1) 3^n,$  find a recurrence relation  $a_n + p a_{n+1} + q a_{n+2} + r a_{n+3} = 0.$  Hence evaluate  $\sum_{n\geq0} a_n x^n.$
solution_md: $$ a_n=(n^2+1)3^n\implies a_{n+1}=(n^2+2n+2)3^{n+1} $$     $$ \implies a_{n+1}-3a_n=(2n+1)3^{n+1}\implies a_{n+2}-3a_{n+1}=(2n+3)3^{n+2} $$     $$ \implies (a_{n+2}-3a_{n+1})-3(a_{n+1}-3a_n)=2\cdot 3^{n+2}\implies a_{n+2}-6a_{n+1}+9a_n=2\cdot 3^{n+2} $$     $$ \implies a_{n+3}-6a_{n+2}+9a_{n+1}=2\cdot 3^{n+3}=3(a_{n+2}-6a_{n+1}+9a_n)\implies 27a_n=a_{n+3}-9a_{n+2}+27a_{n+1} $$     $$ \implies a_n+(-1)a_{n+1}+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)a_{n+2}+\left(-\frac{1}{27}\right)a_{n+3}=0.\quad\quad\quad(*) $$   Define   $$ f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nx^n $$   which has radius of convergence  $1/3.$  So we define  $f(x)$  for  $|x|<1/3.$  Then by  $(*),$    $$ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(a_nx^{n+3}+(-1)a_{n+1}x^{n+3}+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)a_{n+2}x^{n+3}+\left(-\frac{1}{27}\right)a_{n+3}x^{n+3}\right)=0 $$     $$ \implies x^3f(x)+(-1)x^2(f(x)-a_0)+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)x(f(x)-a_0-a_1x)+\left(-\frac{1}{27}\right)(f(x)-a_0-a_1x-a_2x^2)=0 $$     $$ \implies x^3f(x)-(x^2f(x)-x^2)+\left(\frac{xf(x)}{3}-\frac{x}{3}-2x^2\right)-\left(\frac{f(x)}{27}-\frac{1}{27}-\frac{2x}{9}-\frac{5x^2}{3}\right)=0 $$     $$ \implies f(x)(27x^3-27x^2+9x-1)=-18x^2+3x-1\implies f(x)=\frac{1-3x+18x^2}{1-9x+27x^2-27x^3}. $$

solution_md:
The lines of tangency  $x=0$  and  $y=0$ , the line through the points of tangency  $2x+y-2=0$ .
Equation of the conic  $(2x+y-2)^{2}+k \cdot xy=0$ .
This conic is a parabola if  $k=-8$ ,
so our equation  $f(x,y)=(2 \cdot x-1 \cdot y)^{2}-8x-4y+4=0$ .
The axis has equation  $2 \cdot f'_{x}-1 \cdot f'_{y}=0$  or  $2x-y=1.2$ .
Vertex, see previous post.

\[n=\prod_{i=1}^{k} p_{i(1)}p_{i(2)} \dots p_{i(e_i)}\]

By the principle of inclusion-exclusion we have that,

\[P= A \cup B \cup C = A+B+C - A \cap B - B \cap C - A \cap C + A \cap B \cap C\]
Now consider  $F(P)$ .

\[F(P)=F(A \cup B \cup C)=F(A+B+C - A \cap B - B \cap C - A \cap C + A \cap B \cap C)\]
\[F(P)=\frac{F(A)F(B)F(C)F(A \cap B \cap C)}{F(A \cap B)F(B \cap C)F(A \cap C)}\]

Using the properties of  $F(X)$ , this simplifies to

\[lcm(a,b,c)=\frac{abc \cdot \gcd(a,b,c)}{\gcd(a,b) \gcd(b,c) \gcd(a,c)}\]

Squaring and division yields the desired result.

stem_md: A given tetrahedron  $ ABCD$  is isoceles, that is,  $ AB\equal{}CD$ ,  $ AC\equal{}BD$ ,  $ AD\equal{}BC$ . Show that the faces of the tetrahedron are acute-angled triangles.
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>It follows immediately that the sum of the face angles at any vertex is  $ 180^\circ$ .  Since the sum of any two angles of a trihedral angle is greater than the third, each angle must be acute.  If not, assume that  $ \triangle BDC$  is not acute.  Denote the midpoint of  $ \overline{BC}$  by  $ M$ .  Since  $ \triangle ABC \cong \triangle DCB$ ,  $ AM\equal{}DM$ .  Consider the circle with  $ M$  as center and  $ BC$  as diameter.  Since  $ \angle BDC$  is nonacute,  $ C$  must lie within or on the circle.  Thus,  $ 2DM \le BC$ .  By the Triangle Inequality on  $ \triangle AMD$ ,  $ AM\plus{}MD > AD$ .  But  $ AM\equal{}MD$  and  $ AD\equal{}BC$ < so we obtain a contradiction.  Hence, the assumption was false and the assertion in the problem is true.</details>

stem_md: A random selector can only select one of the nine integers  $ 1,2,\ldots,9$ , and it makes these selections with equal probability. Determine the probability that after  $ n$  selections ( $ n>1$ ), the product of the  $ n$  numbers selected will be divisible by 10.
solution_md:
We want the complement of the probability that no multiple of 2 or 5 ever shows up. By PIE, this is just
\[ \boxed{1-\left(\frac{5}{9}\right)^n-\left(\frac{8}{9}\right)^n+\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^n}. \ \blacksquare\]

stem_md: Let  $ R$  denote a non-negative rational number. Determine a fixed set of integers  $ a,b,c,d,e,f$ , such that for *every* choice of  $ R$ , \[ \left| \frac{aR^2\plus{}bR\plus{}c}{dR^2\plus{}eR\plus{}f}\minus{}\sqrt[3]{2}\right| < \left|R\minus{}\sqrt[3]{2}\right|.\]
solution_md:
SolutionWe wish to determine fixed $ a,b,c,d,e,f$ to satisfy the inequality for all nonnegative rational $ R$ . As $ R \rightarrow \sqrt[3]{2}$ through a sequence of rational numbers, the right hand side of this inequality approaches zero. Consequently, the left hand side must vanish if we set $ R\equal{}\sqrt[3]{2}$ . Hence, \[ a \cdot 2^{\frac{2}{3}} \plus{} b \cdot 2^{\frac{1}{3}} \plus{} c \equal{} 2d \plus{} e \cdot 2^{\frac{2}{3}} \plus{} f \cdot 2^{\frac{1}{3}}.\] It follows that $ a\equal{}e$ , $ b\equal{}f$ , $ c\equal{}2d$ . On substituting back into the inequality and factoring out the common factor $ R \minus{} \sqrt[3]{2}$ from both sides, we obtain \[ \left | \frac{aR \plus{} b\minus{}d \cdot 2^{\frac{1}{3}} \left (R \plus{} 2^{\frac{1}{3}} \right )}{dR^2\plus{}aR\plus{}b} \right | < 1.\] For the last inequality to be satisfied, it suffices to let $ a,b,d$ be positive integers and make the numerator nonnegative, i.e., by letting $ a>d \cdot 2^{\frac{1}{3}}$ , $ b > d \cdot 2^{\frac{2}{3}}$ . A simple choice is $ d\equal{}1$ , $ a\equal{}b\equal{}2$ , leading to \[ \frac{2R^2\plus{}2R\plus{}2}{R^2\plus{}2R\plus{}2}.\]

Also, the numerator by your selection of numbers is nonnegative at d=1, a=b=2, and denominator is nonnegative trivially since R is nonnegative and b=2 is also nonnegative. stem_md: A given convex pentagon  $ ABCDE$  has the property that the area of each of five triangles  $ ABC, BCD, CDE, DEA$ , and  $ EAB$  is unity *(equal to 1)*. Show that all pentagons with the above property have the same area, and calculate that area. Show, furthermore, that there are infinitely many non-congruent pentagons having the above area property.
solution_md:
SolutionLet $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ be the probability that the product does not include an even number and the probability that the product does not include the number $5$ , respectively. Notice that in order for the final product to be divisible by $10$ , it must include an even number and the number $5$ . Thus, we want the complement of $P(A\cup B)$ . By PIE, $1-P(A\cup B)=1-(P(A)+P(A)-P(A\cap B)=1-((\frac{8}{9})^n+(\frac{5}{9})^n-(\frac{4}{9})^n).\blacksquare$

stem_md: Two points  $ P$  and  $ Q$  lie in the interior of a regular tetrahedron  $ ABCD$ . Prove that angle  $ PAQ < 60^\circ$ .
solution_md:
Suppose $AP$ and $AQ$ intersect the plane $BCD$ at points $X$ and $Y$ . It is clear that $X$ and $Y$ lie inside the triangle $\bigtriangleup BCD$ . Suppose that the line $XY$ intersects the sides of $\bigtriangleup BCD$ at $S$ and $T$ . WLOG, $S$ is on $BC$ and $T$ is on $BD$ . It is clear that $\angle XAY< \angle SAT$ , and equality cannot occur as the points $P$ and $Q$ cannot lie on the faces of the tetrahedron. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $BC$ and $BD$ respectively, and suppose $S$ and $T$ are a distance $p$ and $q$ from $M$ and $N$ respectively. [asy] size(8cm); pair B = dir(90); pair C = dir(210); pair D = dir(330); pair M = (B+C)/2; pair N = (B+D)/2; pair P = 0.7*B+0.3*C; pair PP = B+C-P; pair Q = 0.4*B+0.6*D; draw(P--Q--PP); draw(B--C--D--B--cycle); dot(" $B$ ",B,dir(B)); dot(" $C$ ",C,dir(C)); dot(" $D$ ",D,dir(D)); dot(" $M$ ",M,dir(M)); dot(" $N$ ",N,dir(N)); dot(" $S$ ",P,dir(P)); dot(" $S'$ ",PP,dir(PP)); dot(" $T$ ",Q,dir(Q)); [/asy] Suppose that $S$ is in segment $BM$ . Then noting that $\cos\angle SAT=\frac{AS^2+AT^2-ST^2}{2AS\cdot AT}$ , we may reflect $S$ over $M$ to get $S'$ . The quantity $ST$ increases (since $S$ is on the same side as $T$ on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ ), and the angle $\angle SAT$ also increases. Similarly, we may assume that $T$ lies in segment $BN$ . Letting the tetrahedron have side length 2, we have $$ ST^2=BS^2+BT^2-2BS\cdot BT\cos\angle SBT =(1+p)^2+(1+q)^2-(1+p)(1+q)=(1+2p+p^2+1+2q+q^2)-(1+p+q+pq) =p^2+q^2+pq+p+q+1 $$ Thus, $$ \cos\angle SAT=\frac{3+p^2+3+q^2-(p^2+q^2+pq+p+q+1)}{2\sqrt{(3+p^2)(3+q^2)}}=\frac{5-pq-p-q}{2\sqrt{(3+p^2)(3+q^2)}} $$ As $p$ increases, the numerator is strictly decreasing while the denominator is strictly increasing, thus $\cos \angle SAT$ is decreasing and $\angle SAT$ is increasing. Thus we may position $S$ at vertex $C$ to maximise $\angle SAT$ . Similarly, $T$ is at vertex $D$ to maximise $\angle SAT$ . Thus, $\angle PAQ < \angle SAT \leq 60^{\circ}$ .
In your last step for simplifying the expression for $ST^2$ , you flipped the sign of $pq$ . It should be \[ST^2 = p^2 + q^2 - pq + p + q + 1. \] Thus, unfortunately, the last step of your proof is also not true. Or rather it needs to be fixed: \[cos SAT = \frac{4 + (p-1)(q-1)}{2\sqrt{(3+p^2)(3+q^2)}}.\] Since half the edge length of the tetrahedron in your proof is 1, and $q < 1$ and $p < 1$ since they are distances to the midpoints. both the quantities $p-1$ and $q-1$ are negative. I'll see if this proof is fixable later. Edit: Since in $(p-1)(q-1),$ $p$ and $q$ both lie in the interval $(0,1)$ , we may rewrite as $(1-p)(1-q)$ . As $p$ or $q$ increases, the numerator decreases strictly. Then the proof is complete as above.

Let  $ \{X_n\}$  and  $ \{Y_n\}$  denote two sequences of integers defined as follows:
\begin{align*} X_0 \equal{} 1,\ X_1 \equal{} 1,\ X_{n \plus{} 1} \equal{} X_n \plus{} 2X_{n \minus{} 1} \quad (n \equal{} 1,2,3,\ldots), 
Y_0 \equal{} 1,\ Y_1 \equal{} 7,\ Y_{n \plus{} 1} \equal{} 2Y_n \plus{} 3Y_{n \minus{} 1} \quad (n \equal{} 1,2,3,\ldots).\end{align*}
Prove that, except for the "1", there is no term which occurs in both sequences.
solution_md:
This is probably overkill, but I still like it :)
SolutionWe convert to explicit form. The first recursion can be expressed in the form $X_n=A(2)^n + B (-1)^n$ , so $1=A+B$ and $1=2A-B$ , or $A=\frac{2}{3}$ , $B=\frac{1}{3}$ . The explicit form is therefore $X_n=\frac{2}{3}(2^n)+\frac{1}{3}(-1)^n$ . Similarly, we express the second recursion in the form $Y_n=C(3^n)+D(-1)^n$ , so $1=C+D$ , $7=3C-D$ or $A=2$ , $B=-1$ . The explicit form is therefore $2(3^n)-1(-1)^n$ . Equating these and simplifying, we obtain $3^{n+1}=2(-1)^n+2^n$ . Via simple bounding, we always have $2(-1)^n+2^n < 3^{n+1}$ if $n>0$ , meaning that there is no term apart from the $1$ that appears in both sequences. $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Three distinct vertices are chosen at random from the vertices of a given regular polygon of  $ (2n\plus{}1)$  sides. If all such choices are equally likely, what is the probability that the center of the given polygon lies in the interior of the triangle determined by the three chosen random points?
solution_md: This problem has appeared several times before, and notably in a well known problem on the Putnam contest, I think, where it gave a sphere, and told you to take four points making a tetrahedron and compute the probability it contains the center. First, we can circumscribe a circle around it. Label this polygon's vertices, starting with $A_1$ , and going clockwise, $A_2, A_3, ... , A_{2n}, A_{2n+1}$ . We will proceed by complementary counting. Specifically, we will count the number of triangles that do not have center $O$ as its vertex and has $A_1$ as its "most counterclockwise vertex". In order for those two conditions to be met, we can choose our next two vertices among only the vertices $A_2, A_3, ...A_n, A_{n+1}$ . Since these are $n+1-2+1 = n$ possible selections, the number of ways to form such triangles is $\displaystyle {n} \choose {2}$ . $\square$ \square By symmetry, this property applies for all $2n+1$ vertices. Thus, the total number of ways to form a triangle from 3 vertices of this regular polygon such that it does not contain center $O$ in its interior is $\displaystyle {n} \choose {2}$ $(2n+1)$ . Finally, note that there are $\displaystyle {2n+1} \choose {3}$ total triangles. Since we are counting the complement, we must subtract from 1; thus, our desired probability is: $1- \frac{\frac{(n)(n-1)(2n+1)}{2}}{\frac{(2n+1)(2n)(2n-1)}{6}} = 1-\frac{3n-3}{4n-2}=\boxed{\frac{n+1}{2(2n-1)}} $ . $\blacksquare$ \blacksquare Also, could someone pm/comment on this thread how to latex add a black square/white square at the end of my proof?

In order for those two conditions to be met, we can choose our next two vertices among only the vertices  $A_2, A_3, ...A_n, A_{n+1}$ . Since these are  $n+1-2+1 = n$  possible selections, the number of ways to form such triangles is  $\displaystyle {n} \choose {2}$ .

By symmetry, this property applies for all  $2n+1$  vertices. Thus, the total number of ways to form a triangle from 3 vertices of this regular polygon such that it does not contain center  $O$  in its interior is  $\displaystyle {n} \choose {2}$  $(2n+1)$ .

Finally, note that there are  $\displaystyle {2n+1} \choose {3}$  total triangles.

Since we are counting the complement, we must subtract from 1; thus, our desired probability is: $1- \frac{\frac{(n)(n-1)(2n+1)}{2}}{\frac{(2n+1)(2n)(2n-1)}{6}} = 1-\frac{3n-3}{4n-2}=\boxed{\frac{n+1}{2(2n-1)}}

stem_md:
Determine all roots, real or complex, of the system of simultaneous equations
\begin{align*} x+y+z &= 3, 
x^2+y^2+z^2 &= 3, 
x^3+y^3+z^3 &= 3.\end{align*}
solution_md:
SolutionSquaring the first equation and then subtracting the second equation, we get $$ 2(xy+yz+zx)=6 \implies xy+yz+zx=3. $$ Also, multiplying the first two equations and then subtracting the third one, we get \begin{align*} \sum_{\text{sym}} xy^2=6 &\implies (xy+yz+zx)(x+y+z)-3xyz=6 &\implies 3xyz=3 &\implies xyz=1. \end{align*} Hence, by Vieta, the polynomial with the roots $x, y,$ and $z$ is $$ x^2-3x^2+3x-1=(x-1)^3. $$ It results that the only solution $(x,y,z)$ in complex numbers to the given system of equations is $$ (x,y,z)=\boxed{(1,1,1)} $$ because it is easy to check that this solution indeed works. $\square$
Having done [IMO Longlist 1985/19](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h366289), I realize that there's a cleaner solution:
SolutionThe given system of equations can be rephrased as: $$ \begin{cases} x^1+y^1+z^1=1^1+1^1+1^1 x^2+y^2+z^2=1^2+1^2+1^2 x^3+y^3+z^3=1^3+1^3+1^3 \end{cases} $$ Now, by Newton's Sums, if $P(x)$ is the monic cubic with roots $x,y,z$ and $Q(x)$ is the monic cubic with roots $1,1,1,$ we have $$ P(x) \equiv Q(x) \implies (x,y,z)=\boxed{(1,1,1)}. $$ $\square$

stem_md: Show that the cube roots of three distinct prime numbers cannot be three terms (not necessarily consecutive) of an arithmetic progression.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Different</summary>We prove by contradiction.  Assume that there do exist such numbers  $p_1$ ,  $p_2$ , and  $p_3$  such that  $\sqrt[3]{p_1}$ ,  $\sqrt[3]{p_2}$ ,  $\sqrt[3]{p_3}$  form an arithmetic progression.  Then,  $\sqrt[3]{p_1} + ad = \sqrt[3]{p_2}$  and  $\sqrt[3]{p_2} + bd = \sqrt[3]{p_3}$  for common difference  $d$  and integers  $a$ ,  $b$ .  Cubing gives
\begin{align*}p_1 + (ad)^3 + 3ad\sqrt[3]{p_1} \cdot (\sqrt[3]{p_1} + ad) &= p_2 p_2 + (bd)^3 + 3bd\sqrt[3]{p_2} \cdot (\sqrt[3]{p_2} + bd) &= p_3\end{align*}  Plugging in  $\sqrt[3]{p_1} + ad = p_2$  and  $\sqrt[3]{p_2} + bd = p_3$ ,
\begin{align*}3ad\sqrt[3]{p_1} \cdot (\sqrt[3]{p_2}) &= \text{integer} 3bd\sqrt[3]{p_2} \cdot (\sqrt[3]{p_3}) &= \text{integer}\end{align*}  Dividing gives 
\[\frac{a}{b} \cdot \sqrt[3]{\frac{p_1}{p_3}} = \text{rational} \Longrightarrow \sqrt[3]{\frac{p_1}{p_3}} = \text{rational}\]  But this is impossible because  $p_1$  and  $p_3$  don't share any factors besides 1, and no prime numbers are perfect cubes.  Contradiction.</details>

solution_md:
As  $a$ , $b$  and  $c\in \mathbb{R^+}$  and  $a$ , $b$  and  $c>0$ ,by the AM-GM inequality ,\[a+b+c\ge 3(abc)^\frac{1}{3}\].
Taking logarithm on both sides, we have \[\log \frac{a+b+c}{3}\ge \frac{1}{3} (\log a+ \log b+\log c)\dots \boxed{1}\]

Now consider the function  $f(x)=x\log x$ . $f''>0$ , i.e.  $f$  is convex.So by Jensen's inequality, we get \[\frac{1}{3}(a \log a+b\ log b+c \log c)\ge \frac{a+b+c}{3}\log (\frac{a+b+c}{3})\]
\[\ge \frac{1}{3} (\log a+ \log b+\log c)\cdot \frac{a+b+c}{3}\](using  $\boxed{1}$ ) which gives us the desired inequality on simplification. $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
A father, a mother and son hold a family tournament, playing a two person board game with no ties. The tournament rules are:
(i) The weakest player chooses the first two contestants.
(ii) The winner of any game plays the next game against the person left out.
(iii) The first person to win two games wins the tournament.
The father is the weakest player, the son the strongest, and it is assumed that any player's probability of winning an individual game from another player does not change during the tournament.
Prove that the father's optimal strategy for winning the tournament is to play the first game with his wife.
solution_md:
Let  $p$  be the probability that the father beats the mother, let  $q$  be the probability that the father beats the son, and let  $r$  be the probability that the mother beats the son. By the "strength" conditions,  $0<p,q,r<1/2.$  and  $q<p,r$ .

Note that if the father plays the mother first, the probability of winning is   $$ p(q+(1-q)rp)+(1-p)(1-r)qp=2pq+rp-2pqr-p^2q+p^2qr. $$   Similarly, if he plays the son first, the probability of winning is   $$ q(p+(1-p)(1-r)q)+(1-q)pqr=pq+q^2-pq^2-rq^2+pqr. $$  Therefore, it suffices to prove the inequality   $$ 2pq+rp-2pqr-p^2q+p^2qr\geq pq+q^2-pq^2-rq^2+pqr $$   for positive reals  $0<p,q,r<1/2$  with  $q<p,r.$  (the case where the father lets the other two play is  $pq$ , which is clearly smaller than both of these). This can be rearranged to   $$ pq+rp+p^2qr+pq^2+rq^2\geq q^2+3pqr+p^2q. $$   We will instead prove the stronger result   $$ pq+rp+pq^2+rq^2\geq q^2+3pqr+p^2q $$   (the  $p^2qr$  term was removed from the left). Note that this can be expressed as   $$ r(p+q^2-3pq)+pq+pq^2\geq q^2+p^2q. $$   Since this is linear in  $r$ , it suffices to prove the inequality for the two "extreme" values, which we will use  $r=0$  and  $r=1/2$  as the extreme values.

For  $r=0$ , we want to prove that   $$ pq+pq^2\geq q^2+p^2q. $$   Reducing by  $q$ , this becomes   $$ p+pq\geq q+p^2, $$   which rearranges to   $$ p(1-p)\geq q(1-p), $$   which is clearly true as we know  $q<p$ .

For  $r=1/2$  we want to prove that   $$ (1/2)(p+q^2-3pq)+pq+pq^2\geq q^2+p^2q $$     $$ p+2pq^2\geq q^2+2p^2q+pq. $$   Note that since  $pq\geq q^2$ , it suffices to show that   $$ p+2pq^2\geq pq+2p^2q+pq. $$   Reducing by  $p$ , this is   $$ 1+2q^2\geq 2q+2pq. $$   However, note that  $1>2p$ , so it suffices to show that   $$ p+q^2\geq q+pq. $$   This rearranges to   $$ p(1-q)\geq q(1-q), $$   which is clearly true, so we are finally done.

solution_md:
Are there any shorter solutions?
I believe algebra bashing is the only viable option. Although it could be made shorter by the usage of a nice formula. By the sine area formula, we have that $[ABC]=[ADC]+[BDC]+[BDA]=\frac{1}{2} \sin{120^{\circ}}(uv + vw + wu) = \frac{(uv + vw + wu) \sqrt{3}}{4}$ . Now by LoC, we have that $a^2=v^2+vw+w^2,b^2=w^2+wu+u^2,c^2=u^2+uv+v^2$ . Now we apply the rarely useful formula ( I probably wouldn't do this in contest ) but here goes: In general, if you have an equilateral triangle of side $x$ and the distances of a point inside to the three vertices are $a,b,c$ , then $x^2=\frac{1}{2}(a^2+b^2+c^2)+2\sqrt{3} \Delta$ where $\Delta$ is the area of a triangle with side $a,b,c$ . More information can be found [here](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2758901/edge-length-of-an-equilateral-triangle-if-distances-from-a-point-p-to-its-vert#:~:text=In%20general%2C%20if%20you%20have,side%20a%2Cb%2Cc.). This gives $x^2=\frac{1}{2}(v^2+vw+w^2+w^2+wu+u^2+u^2+uv+v^2)+2\sqrt{3} \frac{(uv + vw + wu) \sqrt{3}}{4}$ , which simplifies to $x^2=\frac{1}{2}(2u^2+2v^2+2w^2+uv+vw+wu)+\frac{3(uv + vw + wu)}{2}$ . Now we split the large fraction into $x^2=\frac{1}{2}(uv+vw+wu)+u^2+v^2+w^2+\frac{3(uv + vw + wu)}{2}$ , which then simplifies into $x^2=u^2+v^2+w^2+2(uv+vw+wu)$ . However, we notice that the right hand side is simply $(u+v+w)^2$ , so thus we have $\boxed{x=u+v+w}$ . .

(a) Prove that \[ [5x]\plus{}[5y] \ge [3x\plus{}y] \plus{} [3y\plus{}x],\] where  $ x,y \ge 0$  and  $ [u]$  denotes the greatest integer  $ \le u$  (e.g.,  $ [\sqrt{2}]\equal{}1$ ).
(b) Using (a) or otherwise, prove that \[ \frac{(5m)!(5n)!}{m!n!(3m\plus{}n)!(3n\plus{}m)!}\] is integral for all positive integral  $ m$  and  $ n$ .
solution_md:
A detailed proof for part  $a)$ :

If  $(x,y)$  satisfies this inequality, then  it is easy to see that  $(x+1,y)$  and  $(x,y+1)$  also satisfy.

So we can assume that  $x,y \in [0,1)$  $\frac{k-1}{5} \leq x < \frac{k}{5} \: , \: \frac{l-1}{5} \leq y < \frac{l}{5}$  where  $k,l \in \{1,2,3,4,5\}$  $3k+l \equiv u \pmod{5} \: , \: k+3l \equiv v \pmod{5} \: , \: u,v \in \{1,2,3,4,5\}$  $\Longrightarrow \; \lfloor 5x \rfloor = k-1 \; , \; \lfloor 5y \rfloor = l-1$  and  $ \lfloor 3x+y \rfloor = \frac{3k+l-u}{5} \; , \; \lfloor x+3y \rfloor = \frac{k+3l-v}{5}$ The inequality is equivalent to $k+l+u+v \geq 10$   $3k+l \equiv u \pmod{5} \: , \: k+3l \equiv v \pmod{5} \; \Longrightarrow$  $k+l+u+v \equiv 0 \pmod{5} \; , \; k+l+u+v>0$  $k+l+u+v=5 \; \Longrightarrow \; (k,l,u,v)$  is some permutation of  $(1,1,1,2)$  $k=l=1 \; \Longrightarrow \; u \equiv 4 \pmod{5}$   $k=1\; , \; l=2 \; \Longrightarrow \; u \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$  $k=2 \; , \; l=1 \; \Longrightarrow \; v \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$  $\Longrightarrow \; k+l+u+v \neq 5$  and solution is done. :wink:

On plugging k = -1 in the above equation to eliminate the (k + 1).p(k) term and get the value of the leading coefficient a, we get

1 = a(-1)(-2)(-3)........(-1 - n)

a[(-1)^n + 1 (n + 1)!] = 1

a = (-1)^n + 1/(n + 1)!

Now, On plugging k = n + 1 in the same equation, we get 

(n + 2).p(n + 1) -(n + 1) = a[(n + 1).n.(n - 1).........1]

(n + 2).p(n + 1) -(n + 1) = a(n + 1)!

(n + 2).p(n + 1) -(n + 1) = (-1)^n + 1

(n + 2).p(n + 1) = (-1)^n + 1 + (n + 1)

Therefore, p(n + 1) = [(-1)^n + 1 + (n + 1)]/(n + 2)

If n is odd then p(n + 1) = 1 and if n is even then p(n + 1) = n/n + 2

stem_md: A deck of  $ n$  playing cards, which contains three aces, is shuffled at random (it is assumed that all possible card distributions are equally likely). The cards are then turned up one by one from the top until the second ace appears. Prove that the expected (average) number of cards to be turned up is  $ (n\plus{}1)/2$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary> another way</summary>The probability that the  $ m^{th}$  card is the second ace is given by $ P(m) \equal{} (m \minus{} 1)\left(\frac {3}{n}\cdot\frac {n \minus{} 3}{n \minus{} 1}\cdot\frac {n \minus{} 4}{n \minus{} 2}\cdot\cdot\cdot\frac {n \minus{} m}{n \minus{} m \plus{} 2}\right)\frac {2}{n \minus{} m \plus{} 1}$  $ \equal{} 6(m \minus{} 1)\frac {(n \minus{} m)!}{n!}\frac {(n \minus{} 3)!}{(n \minus{} m \minus{} 1)!} \equal{} \frac {(n \minus{} m)(m \minus{} 1)}{\binom{n}{3}}$ Where  $ 2\le m \le n \minus{} 1$ Therefore  $ E(x) \equal{} \sum_{k \equal{} 2}^{n \minus{} 1} kP(k)$  $ \equal{} \frac {1}{\binom{n}{3}} \sum_{k \equal{} 2}^{n \minus{} 1} k(n \minus{} k)(k \minus{} 1)$ For  $ n$  odd

There is symmetry in the expression  $ p(m) \equal{} m(n \minus{} m)(m \minus{} 1)$ , that is  $ p(k) \plus{} p(n \minus{} k) \equal{} (n \minus{} 2)(n \minus{} k)k$  $ \therefore \sum_{k \equal{} 2}^{n \minus{} 1} k(n \minus{} k)(k \minus{} 1) \equal{} (n \minus{} 1)P(n \minus{} 1) \plus{} (n \minus{} 2)\sum_{k \equal{} 2}^{\frac {n \minus{} 1}{2}}k(n \minus{} k)$  $ \equal{} (n \minus{} 2)\left((n \minus{} 1) \plus{} \frac {(n \minus{} 1)(n^2 \plus{} n \minus{} 12)}{12}\right) \equal{} \frac {(n \minus{} 2)(n \minus{} 1)n(n \plus{} 1)}{12}$ For  $ n$  even

The symetry is  $ p(k) \plus{} p(n \minus{} k \plus{} 1) \equal{} (k \minus{} 1)(n \minus{} k)(n \plus{} 1)$   $ \therefore \sum_{k \equal{} 2}^{n \minus{} 1} k(n \minus{} k)(k \minus{} 1) \equal{} (n \plus{} 1)\sum_{k \equal{} 2}^{\frac {n}{2}}(k \minus{} 1)(n \minus{} k)$  $ \equal{} (n \plus{} 1)\left(\frac {x(x \minus{} 2)(x \minus{} 1)}{12}\right) \equal{} \frac {(n \minus{} 2)(n \minus{} 1)n(n \plus{} 1)}{12}$  $ \therefore E(x) \equal{} \frac {1}{\binom{n}{3}}\frac {(n \minus{} 2)(n \minus{} 1)n(n \plus{} 1)}{12} \equal{} \boxed{\frac {n \plus{} 1}{2}}$</details>

stem_md:
(a) Suppose that each square of a 4 x 7 chessboard is colored either black or white. Prove that with *any* such coloring, the board must contain a rectangle (formed by the horizontal and vertical lines of the board) whose four distinct unit corner squares are all of the same color.
(b) Exhibit a black-white coloring of a 4 x6 board in which the four corner squares of every rectangle, as described above, are not all of the same color.
solution_md: (a) Note that there are  $\binom 5 2  \binom 8 2 = 280$  total possible rectangles in the chessboard. However, there are only  $2^7 \cdot 2 = 2^8$  possibilities for the rectangle itself since the choosing of the first row determines the second row, so thus by Pigeonhole we are done.  $\blacksquare$ (b) insert counterexample

stem_md: Determine all integral solutions of \[ a^2\plus{}b^2\plus{}c^2\equal{}a^2b^2.\]
solution_md:
Rearranging, we find
\[c^2+1 = (a^2-1)(b^2-1).\]

Fermat's Christmas Theorem tells us all factors of the LHS with magnitude greater than 1 must be 1 or 2 modulo 4, contradiction. Thus  $c^2+1 \leq 1 \implies c=0$ , giving the only solution  $\boxed{(0,0,0)}$ .  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: If the sum of the lengths of the six edges of a trirectangular tetrahedron  $ PABC$  (i.e.,  $ \angle APB \equal{} \angle BPC \equal{} \angle CPA \equal{} 90^\circ$ ) is  $ S$ , determine its maximum volume.
solution_md:
hello, let  $ \overline{PB} \equal{} a,\overline{PA} \equal{} b,\overline{PC} \equal{} c$  then we get the volume of our trirectangular tetraeder in the form of $ V \equal{} \frac {1}{6}abc\le\left(\frac {a \plus{} b \plus{} c}{3}\right)^{\frac {1}{3}}$  after AM-GM. Further we can compute  $ s$  with the Pythagorean theorem as $ s \equal{} a \plus{} b \plus{} c \plus{} \sqrt {a^2 \plus{} b^2} \plus{} \sqrt {a^2 \plus{} c^2} \plus{} \sqrt {b^2 \plus{} c^2}$  since  $ \frac {x \plus{} y}{2}\le\sqrt {\frac {x^2 \plus{} y^2}{2}}$  we get $ s\geq(\sqrt {2} \plus{} 1)(a \plus{} b \plus{} c)$  so our  $ V$  can be estimate as $ V \equal{} \frac {1}{6}abc\le\frac {1}{6}\left(\frac {a \plus{} b \plus{} c}{3}\right)^{\frac {1}{3}}\le \frac {1}{6}\left(\frac {s}{3(\sqrt {2} \plus{} 1)}\right)^{\frac {1}{3}}$ .
Sonnhard.

solution_md:
My StartNote that if $1$ is a root of $P(x)$ , then $x-1$ must be a factor of $P(x)$ . Plugging in $x=1$ to the original equation, we get $P(1)+Q(1)+R(1)=5S(1)$ . Plugging in $x=0$ gives $P(0)=S(0)$ .

There is a way. Let $T\colon\mathbb R[x]\to\mathbb R^5$ be the function given by \[ \sum a_kx^k\mapsto\left(\sum_{5\mid k}a_k,\sum_{5\mid k-1}a_k,\ldots,\sum_{5\mid k-4}a_k\right). \] It is clear that \[ T(P(x^5)+xQ(x^5)+x^2R(x^5))=(P(1),Q(1),R(1),0,0). \] It is also easy to see that \[ T((x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1)S(x))=(S(1),S(1),S(1),S(1),S(1)). \] Since $P(x^5)+xQ(x^5)+x^2R(x^5)=(x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1)S(x)$ , these two must be equal, giving \[ P(1)=Q(1)=R(1)=S(1)=0. \] Hence, $x-1\mid P(x)$ . $\blacksquare$

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $ x^{m\plus{}1}\equal{}1$  with  $ x\ne{1}$ . Then, as the second polynomial is equal to zero, we must also have the first polynomial equal to zero.

We shall show that  $ n$  and  $ m\plus{}1$  must be relatively prime. Suppose that there is a common divisor of both,  $ k$ , that is greater than  $ 1$ . Then clearly  $ \frac{m\plus{}1}{k}\le{m}$ , meaning that there will be at least one number among  $ n, 2n, ... mn$  that is divisible by  $ m\plus{}1$ , which we cannot have. Thus,  $ m\plus{}1$  and  $ n$  must be relatively prime.</details>
